cards.front: What is a retrovirus?

cards.back:
Provirus**:** Viral DNA integrated into a eukaryotic cell’s genome (e.g., human).

➤ Common in ***retroviruses*** like HIV.

➤ Requires ***reverse transcriptase*** to convert RNA to DNA.

Prophage**:** Bacteriophage DNA integrated into a bacterial genome.

➤ Part of the ***lysogenic cycle*** in bacteria.

➤ Can later reactivate and enter the ***lytic cycle.***

cards.front: What drives breathing?

cards.back:
1. Diaphragm flattens (contracts) - **thoracic cavity V increases.**

2. Intrapleural space increases as outer parietal membrane is pulled down w/ diaphragm, but visceral membrane stays attached to lungs.

3. Intrapleural V increases, so P decreases --> lowers external pressure compressing lungs

4. This allows lungs to expand, pushing the pleurae further outward

5. Lung V increases, **P decreases creates pressure gradient** from atm pressure outside to lung pressure inside

6. Air rushes into lungs from outside down the pressure gradient and alveoli are filled for gas exchange.

Means we *decrease* pressure inside lungs so air rushes in - by reducing pressure we suck air into lungs

We *don't* increase pressure outside lungs/body --> that's ridiculous lol

Follows Boyle's law!
![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1051.png)
cards.front: What is meant by negative pressure breathing?

cards.back:
**Both active and passive**

Exhalation can be passive as in the case of the diaphragm and external intercostals relaxing, causing the size of the chest cavity to decrease, and increasing the pressure there in.

In certain times of need/pathology, exhalation can be active. This is when muscles are recruited to increase the force of contraction on the lungs and to help in forcing air out of the lungs.
cards.front: Exhalation is a [active, passive, or both] process

cards.back:
1. Contracted diaphragm relaxes

2. Chest cavity decreases in volume, increasing its pressure.

3. Higher external pressure causes the lungs to decrease in volume, **increasing their pressure.**

4. Higher pressure air in the lungs travels down its pressure gradient to the outside world.

Note, this is just the reverse of inhalation.
This is also a passive process, muscles are being allowed to passively relax instead of being actively contracted.
cards.front: How do we exhale?

cards.back:
**Inhalation**

They expand up+outward --> brings with it parietal pleurae
This increases volume (dec pressure) in intrapleural space
= Visceral pleurae + lung expands into it

cards.front: What are the characteristics of capillaries?

cards.back:
1. Thin walled, not very muscular, and inelastic.

2. Not resistive - take **larger amount of volume at slower rate**
3/4s of blood in body is usually in veins

3. Have valves to prevent the backflow of blood

cards.front: What are the three characteristics of veins?

cards.back:
Veins don't push blood forward w/ their elasticity

Instead they're** acted upon by surrounding skeletal muscle contractions** --> slowly squeeze blood forward

They fight against gravity, and b/c they're slower, much more likely blood will flow backwards
**Venous valves protect against this**
cards.front: Why does it make sense that veins have valves?

cards.back:
1. Right atrium --> tricuspid valve --> right ventricle

2. Right ventricle --> pulmonary valve --> pulmonary artery

3. Pulmonary artery --> lungs --> pulmonary veins

4. Pulmonary veins --> left atrium

5. Left atrium --> bicuspid (mitral) valve --> left ventricle

6. Left ventricle --> aortic valve --> aorta

7. Arteries --> arterioles --> capillaries --> venules --> veins

8. Veins --> vena cava --> right atrium

cards.front: What are Starling Forces?

cards.back:
Hydrostatic pressure = high on arteriole side of capillary bed

Decreases as blood moves across the bed into venules

Oncotic pressure is constant through entirety of capillary bed
This means that on arteriole side, there's a net force out of the vasculature into the tissues

On venule side, hydrostatic force is too low, so net force is from tissues into vasculature

Oncotic pressure, on the other hand, is constant throughout the entirety of the capillaryt bed.

This means that, on the arteriole side of the bed, there is a net force out of the vasculature into the tissues.

On the venule side of the capillary bed, the hydrostatic force is too low, and the net force is not from the tissues into the vasculature.

**X-axis:** pO₂ **Y-axis:** Hemoglobin O₂ saturation

In **lungs** (**high O₂ pp**) → Hb is ~100% saturated

In **tissues** (low O₂ pp, e.g. exercising muscle) → Hb releases O₂

Curve shows how *Hb holds O₂ in high-O₂ areas and releases it where it's needed most*

cards.front: How do the X and Y axis of the hemoglobin dissociation curve explain the way hemoglobin is delivered to tissues?

cards.back:
The curve is sigmoidal due to cooperative binding.

Small changes in pO₂ (e.g. ~20 mmHg between resting and exhausted muscle) cause large changes in O₂ release.

At higher pO₂ (resting muscle), hemoglobin holds O₂; at lower pO₂ (exercising muscle), it rapidly unloads O₂

The body can shift the curve (e.g. via pH, CO₂) to enhance delivery during high demand.

cards.front: How does cooperative binding make hemoglobin a very efficient oxygen delivery system?

cards.back:
The Bohr effect is a rightward shift in the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve due to:

↑ CO₂ concentration --> means **more carbonic acid, which lowers pH**

↑ H⁺ (↓ pH) --> lower pH (more acidic) **reduces hemoglobin’s oxygen affinity**

↑ Temperature --> higher temps, like in working muscles, **also reduce O₂ affinity

**MNEMONIC: **Exercise** is the **right** thing to do! Exercise increases your CO2 concentration, decreases your blood pH, and increases your temperature.

cards.front: What is the Bohr effect?

cards.back:
No.

At the higher end of the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve, where the partial pressure of oxygen is high (like in the lungs) hemoglobin will be close to 100% saturated, even if the curve has been shifted. However, at the low end of the curve, where partial pressure of oxygen is low, the saturation of hemoglobin can be significantly different after a shift.

Network of channels that immune cells use to communicate and mount attacks against pathogens.

An **enzyme in the nose, tears, and saliva. **

Complement proteins punch holes in the cell wall of bacteria** causing lysis

When system is activated by binding of antibody to a pathogen

When system is activated without need of an antibody

CD4+ cells that help shut down immune response after infection is cleared

Prevent autoimmunity by **inhibiting self-reactive lymphocytes

Long-lived T cells formed after initial infection

**Recognize the same antigen upon re-exposure**

Enable faster and stronger secondary immune response

Protein and carbohydrate tags on the **surface of our own cells

cards.back:
It treats the self antigen as foreign

**Triggers an immune response** against normal cells

Can lead to *autoimmune disease*

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/high-school-biology/hs-human-body-systems/hs-the-immune-system/v/self-versus-non-self)
cards.front: What happens if the immune system does not recognize a self antigen?

cards.back:
Immune system fails to recognize self antigens

Attacks and destroys healthy body cells

Results in tissue damage and chronic disease

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/high-school-biology/hs-human-body-systems/hs-the-immune-system/v/self-versus-non-self)
cards.front: What is an autoimmune disease?

like cortisol or prednisone

Used to reduce inflammation and treat autoimmune conditions

Inhibit T cells and cytokine production to calm immune responses

cards.back:
1. Active immunity

2. Passive immunity
cards.front: What are the two ways immunity to a disease can be acquired?

cards.back:
You already have memory cells and antibodies against it

The infection may still occur, but it's **cleared so quickly that symptoms are minimal or absent**
cards.front: What does it mean to be immune to a disease?

cards.back:
Immunity developed after exposure to a pathogen

Can be **natural** (**infection**) or **artificial** (**vaccination**)

Body produces its own antibodies and memory cells

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/test-prep/mcat/organ-systems/the-immune-system/v/types-of-immune-responses-innate-and-adaptive-humoral-vs-cell-mediated)
cards.front: What is active immunity?

cards.back:
Expose the body to a weakened or inactive form of a pathogen

**Trigger antibody and memory cell production** without causing disease

"Train" the immune system for faster future responses
cards.front: How do vaccines work?

cards.back:
Immunity from receiving antibodies made by another person or organism

Provides **immediate**, **short**-**term protection** (e.g. maternal antibodies, antibody injections)

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3w9ylCxFAa0)
cards.front: What is passive immunity?

cards.back:
The Immune system has been exposed to the pathogen in Active Immunity, and therefore has the cells that produce antibodies for that pathogen indefinitely

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/test-prep/mcat/organ-systems/the-immune-system/v/types-of-immune-responses-innate-and-adaptive-humoral-vs-cell-mediated)
cards.front: Active immunity is {{c1::permanent::permanent or temporary?}}

cards.back:
The Immune system has not been exposed to the pathogen in Passive Immunity, and therefore does not have the cells that produce antibodies for that pathogen.

The **antibodies that a person receives in passive therapy will eventually break down or run out.
**
[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3w9ylCxFAa0)
cards.front: Passive immunity is {{c1::temporary::permanent or temporary?}}

cards.back:
Circulatory system of vessels that carries lymph through tissues and **returns it to the bloodstream**

Helps maintain fluid balance, filter pathogens, and support immune function

cards.front: What is the lymphatic system?

cards.back:
Small, bean-shaped structures along lymph vessels

Site where immune cells encounter and respond to pathogens in lymph

cards.front: What is a lymph node?

cards.back:
Fluid balance: **Returns excess interstitial fluid to the bloodstream**, ***preventing tissue swelling***

Fat absorption: ***Lacteals*** **in small intestine absorb dietary fats** and ***transport them as chylomicrons***

Immune surveillance: **Lymph nodes filter lymph and expose immune cells to antigens** for activation
cards.front: What are the functions of the lymphatic system as a secondary circulatory system?

cards.back:
Proteins released by virus-infected cells

**Inhibit viral replication and spread**

Help nearby cells resist infection and activate immune defenses

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m683.jpg)

Phagocytosis: Recognize, **engulf**, and **digest** **pathogens** using hydrolytic enzymes

Antigen presentation: **Display pathogen antigens on MHC class II** to ***activate adaptive immunity***

Cytokine release: Secrete **signaling molecules to recruit and activate other immune cells** in affected tissue

cards.front: What are the 3 functions of the Macrophage?

cards.back:
MHC (Major Histocompatibility Complex) is a protein on immune cells like macrophages

It **binds pathogen antigens** and** displays them on cell surface**

Allows adaptive immune cells to recognize and respond to the pathogen

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m202.jpg)

cards.front: What is MHC?

cards.back:
A **signaling protein released by immune cells**

Stimulates inflammation and recruits other immune cells to the site of infection or injury
cards.front: What is a cytokine?

cards.back:
1. MHC Class 1

2. MHC Class 2

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/human-biology/immunology/v/professional-antigen-presenting-cells-apc-and-mhc-ii-complexes)
cards.front: What are the two types of MHC's found in the body?

cards.back:
Found on all nucleated cells

**Present** **intracellular** **antigens** (e.g. from viruses) **on cell surface**

Allow cytotoxic T cells (***CD8⁺***) to detect and destroy infected cells

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/human-biology/immunology/v/professional-antigen-presenting-cells-apc-and-mhc-ii-complexes)
cards.front: Describe Class 1 MHC's

cards.back:
Pathway where **intracellular (internal)** **antigens** are presented on MHC class I
**
**
Allows infected or abnormal cells to display antigens to CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells

**
**

substance (usually a pathogenic protein) that can be detected by antibodies.

Protein that immune cells can use to recognize a cell as foreign or containing foreign invaders

cards.front: What is an antigen?

cards.back:
Pathway where ***extracellular*** antigens are presented on **MHC class II**

Used by professional antigen-presenting cells (e.g. **macrophages**, **dendritic** cells) after phagocytosing and digesting pathogens

Activates ***CD4⁺ helper T cells***

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m965.jpg)
cards.front: What is the exogenous pathway in the context of the immune system?

cards.back:
1. Macrophages (this includes the specific macrophages like microglia, langherns cells, etc.)

2. Dendritic cells in the skin

3. *Some* B-cells

cards.front: What are some of the professional antigen presenting cells that display class 2 MHC's?

cards.back:
Nonspecific cytotoxic lymphocyte in **innate immunity**

Detects cells with ***↓ MHC*** expression (*often due to viral infection or cancer*)

Kills suspicious cells by inducing apoptosis

**Important in tumor and virus-infected cell elimination**

cards.front: What is a natural killer cell?

cards.back:
1. Neutrophils --> die, puss

2. Eosinophils --> parasites

3. Basophils --> histamine

cards.front: Granulocytes are a part of the {{c1::nonspecific immune system::specific or nonspecific immune system?}}

cards.back:
Short-lived phagocytes that target bacteria

Follow chemical signals via **chemotaxis** to infection sites

Engulf and destroy pathogens quickly

Dead neutrophils **make up most of pus at infection sites**

**
**
[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/test-prep/mcat/organ-systems/the-immune-system/a/innate-immunity)**
**
cards.front: What is the function of Neutrophils?

cards.back:
Pus is the collection of dead neutrophils in an infection

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/test-prep/mcat/organ-systems/the-immune-system/a/innate-immunity)
cards.front: Where does pus come from in an infected wound?

cards.back:
Involved in allergic reactions and parasitic infections

Release histamine to trigger inflammation

**Contain bright red-orange granules
**
[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/test-prep/mcat/organ-systems/the-immune-system/a/innate-immunity)
cards.front: What is the function of Eosinophils?

cards.back:
Molecule that dilates blood vessels and increases their permeability

**Helps immune cells** + **fluid** **move into tissue** to promote inflammation

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/human-biology/immunology/v/inflammatory-response)
cards.front: What is histamine?

cards.back: Extracellular pathogens like **bacteria**, **fungi**, and **parasites**.
cards.front: What kind of pathogens is inflammation effective against?

cards.back:
**Contain large purple granules** and are involved in allergic reactions

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/test-prep/mcat/organ-systems/the-immune-system/a/innate-immunity)
cards.front: What is the function of Basophils?

cards.back:
**Tissue-resident cells** that release histamine in response to allergens

*Similar to basophils but found in tissues*

Involved in allergic reactions, wound healing, and defense against pathogens

Can trigger anaphylaxis in severe allergic responses

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/human-biology/immunology/v/inflammatory-response)
cards.front: What is the function of Mast Cells?

cards.back:
Two different types of Lymphocytes.

1. ** B cells**
2. **T cells**
cards.front: What are the two components of the adaptive immune system?

cards.back:
Proteins that bind to specific antigens

**Mark pathogens for destruction** by the immune system

Help neutralize and clear invaders from the body

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m974.jpg)

cards.front: What are antibodies?

Just another way of saying antibody

cards.front: What is an Immunoglobulin [Ig]?

cards.back:
1. 2 identical heavy chains

2. 2 identical light chains

3. An **antigen binding region**

4. A **variabe region** --> ***recognizes specific epitope on an antigen***

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m53.jpg)

cards.front: What are the basic structural components of an antibody?

cards.back:
No

Response depends on type of antigen, antibody, immune cells, location, etc.
cards.front: Is the response to an antibody-antigen binding event always the same?

cards.back:
Just 1.

Luckily, the body has many B-Cells so we can recognize many different antigens.
cards.front: How many antibodies can each individual B cell produce?

cards.back: B-cell that has not yet been exposed to an antigen and created an antibody for it.
cards.front: What is a naive B-cell?

cards.back: Naive B-cells are stored in the lymph nodes
cards.front: Where are naive B-cells stored?

cards.back:
Start to rapidly divide into two types of cells, **plasma** **cells** and **memory**-**B** **cells
**
[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/human-biology/immunology/v/b-lymphocytes-b-cells)
cards.front: What happens when a naive B-cell is exposed to an antigen?

cards.back:
One of the *product cells of activation of naive B cell.*

It's function is to **enter the bloodstream** and produce large amounts of antibodies

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/human-biology/immunology/v/b-lymphocytes-b-cells)
cards.front: What is a plasma cell?

cards.back:
**Long-lived B cell formed after initial exposure** to an antigen

Stays in lymph nodes and responds rapidly if the same antigen returns

**Allows faster, stronger antibody production** on re-exposure

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/human-biology/immunology/v/b-lymphocytes-b-cells)
cards.front: What is a memory B-cell?

cards.back:
Process where B cells mutate their antibody binding regions to improve antigen affinity

**High-affinity B cells survive; low-affinity ones die**

Takes ~10 days to produce a strong, specific antibody

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/test-prep/mcat/organ-systems/the-immune-system/a/adaptive-immunity)
cards.front: What is hypermutation?

cards.back:
The** slow initial response** to a new infection

Naive B cells take time (~7–10 days) to develop effective antibodies
cards.front: What is the primary immune response?

cards.back:
A rapid and strong response to a previously encountered pathogen

**Driven by memory B cells** that quickly produce the correct antibodies

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2182.png)
cards.front: What is the secondary response in the immune system?

cards.back:
Positive selection refers to one of the ways T-cells are selected for maturation.

In positive selection, T cells that are capable of responding to MHC are allowed to mature.

This happens because T cells need to be able to read MHC's so that they can recognize cells to kill.

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/test-prep/mcat/organ-systems/the-immune-system/a/adaptive-immunity)
cards.front: What is positive selection?

cards.back:
Negative selection is one of the ways T-cells are selected for maturation.

In negative selection, T-cells that erroneously target the body's own healthy cells are apoptosed.

This happens because T-cells need to kill dangerous foreign cells, not the body's own cells!

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/test-prep/mcat/organ-systems/the-immune-system/a/adaptive-immunity)
cards.front: What is negative selection?

cards.back:
Thymosin is a peptide hormone secreted by the cells of the Thymus that causes T-cells to mature

1. Helper T-cells2. Suppressor T-cells

Secrete lymphokines to **coordinate immune response**

Recruit and activate other immune cells to enhance their function

cards.front: What is the function of helper T-Cells?

Extracellular infections (e.g. bacteria, fungi, parasites)

They recognize antigens on MHC class II, which **presents phagocytosed extracellular pathogens

cards.front: What kind of infections do Helper-T cells respond to best?

cards.back:
Also called CD8⁺ T cells

**Directly kill infected or abnormal cells** by inducing apoptosis

Recognize antigens on MHC class I (from** intracellular pathogens**)

cards.front: What is the function of Cytotoxic T-Cells?

cards.back:
Intracellular infections, **especially viruses and some bacteria/fungi**
**
**
They **recognize antigens on MHC class I**, which presents proteins from inside infected cells

cards.front: Discuss Leukocyte classes/divisions

cards.back:
When antigen-presenting cell engulfs a bacterium and transports fragment to cell surface, a specific Helper T-cell recognizes it and becomes activated

Then activates specific B-cells that produce the antibody needed to target the same antigen within the body --> this is clonal selection

Now activated B cell differentiates into plasma cells and memory B cells

Plasma cells begin synthesizing free antibodies and releasing them into the blood

Only the B cells that can bind the antigen with high affinity survive, providing a mechanism for generating secificty.

cards.front: What is clonal selection

cards.back:
In thymus, T-lymphocytes are tested against self-antigens (antigens normally expressed in the body)

Any T-cell that reacts to self antigens is destroyed --> this is negative clonal selection
(Prevents autoimmunes)

If they're non-reactive they're released into the lymphoid tissue and circulate around body through the blood and lymphatic fluid

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/test-prep/mcat/organ-systems/the-immune-system/a/adaptive-immunity)
cards.front: Thymus and clonal selection

cards.back:
Helper T cells --> **Recognize APC bound to infectious agent** --> ***Activate B and T cells***

Memory T cells --> Keep **antigen memory**

Suppressor (Regulatory) T cells --> **Negative feedback for immune system** to terminate response

Killer (cytotoxic) T cells --> **Bind and kill antigen** **carrying cells
**
[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/test-prep/mcat/organ-systems/the-immune-system/a/adaptive-immunity)
cards.front: What do T-lymphocytes differentiate into?

cards.back:
Antigen is engulfed by a macrophage (APC)

**Displayed on MHC class II**

Activates helper T cells → **stimulates B and cytotoxic T cells
**
[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=yDAGxVxY-L8)
cards.front: What happens when an antigen is encountered for the first time?

cards.back:
Humoral (antibody-mediated): Involves **B cells** and **antibodies**

Cell-mediated: Involves** cytotoxic T cells** targeting infected cells

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/test-prep/mcat/organ-systems/the-immune-system/v/types-of-immune-responses-innate-and-adaptive-humoral-vs-cell-mediated)
cards.front: What are the two branches of the adaptive immune response?

cards.back:
Undergo genetic recombination to make unique antibodies

Tested against antigen

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/human-biology/immunology/v/b-lymphocytes-b-cells)
cards.front: What do B cells do upon activation?

cards.back:
Plasma cells are activated B cells that secrete antibodies to neutralize or destroy antigens

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/human-biology/immunology/v/b-lymphocytes-b-cells)
cards.front: What is the role of plasma cells?

cards.back:
Store antibody information for future infections

Enable a faster, stronger secondary response

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/human-biology/immunology/v/b-lymphocytes-b-cells)
cards.front: What is the role of memory B cells?

cards.back:
Activated by helper T cells and **antigens presented on MHC class I** of infected cells

***Differentiate*** into active cytotoxic T cells and memory T cells

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/health-and-medicine/human-anatomy-and-physiology/introduction-to-immunology/v/cytotoxic-t-cells)
cards.front: How are cytotoxic T cells activated?

cards.back:
Kill infected cells by **inducing apoptosis** in cells displaying foreign antigens on MHC class I

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/health-and-medicine/human-anatomy-and-physiology/introduction-to-immunology/v/cytotoxic-t-cells)
cards.front: What is the role of cytotoxic T cells?

cards.back:
CD4⁺ cells that coordinate immune response

**Stimulate B cells**, **cytotoxic T cells**, and **memory cell formation via cytokines
**
[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/human-biology/immunology/v/helper-t-cells)
cards.front: What is the role of helper T cells?

cards.back:
Long-lived CD4⁺ cells that respond rapidly to the same antigen during re-exposure

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/human-biology/immunology/v/helper-t-cells)
cards.front: What are memory helper T cells?

cards.back:
Re-exposure to the same antigen

Activates memory B cells, memory T cells, and memory helper T cells for a faster, stronger response

decks.name: Captain Hook MCAT::2 - Biological and Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems::A) Biology::09 The Digestive System

cards.back:
1. Intracellular digestion

2. Extracellular digestion
cards.front: What are the two types of digestion?

cards.back:
Intracellular digestion = breakdown of substances within the cell

Cell takes in material and **digests it for nutrients**

Involves oxidation of glucose and fatty acids for energy

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m4.jpg)
cards.front: What is intracellular digestion?

cards.back:
Extracellular digestion = breakdown of substances outside the cell

Nutrients are **digested externally, then absorbed** by the cell

Occurs in the digestive tract (e.g., stomach)

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1656.jpg)
cards.front: What is extracellular digestion?

cards.back:
Alimentary canal = passageway from mouth to anus

**Divided into sections by sphincters**

Site of extracellular digestion and nutrient absorption

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1493.jpg)
cards.front: What is the alimentary canal?

cards.back:
Sphincter = circular muscle around the alimentary canal

**Contracts to close off sections** of the canal

Controls movement of material between compartments

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2162.jpg)
cards.front: What is a sphincter?

cards.back:
Digestion = breakdown of food into basic organic molecules

Starches → **monosaccharides**

Lipids → **free fatty acids + glycerol**

Proteins → **amino acids**

Necessary because the body can only metabolize simple building blocks found in complex foods

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2392.gif)
cards.front: What is digestion?

cards.back:
Mechanical digestion = **physical breakdown** of large food particles into smaller ones

Chemical digestion = **enzymatic cleavage of chemical bonds** to release usable nutrients

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1243.jpg)
cards.front: What are the two ways digestion can be achieved?

cards.back:
Absorption = transport of digested nutrients into the circulatory system

**Allows distribution of nutrients** to tissues
cards.front: What is absorption?

cards.back:
1. Oral cavity2. Pharynx
3. Esophagus
4. Stomach
5. Small intestine
6. Large intestine
7. Rectum

**Propels food forward** through the digestive system

cards.front: What is peristalsis?

cards.back:

**Increases secretion from digestive glands**

Enhances peristalsis to move food through GI tract
cards.front: What role does the parasympathetic system play in digestion?
All of the glands of the body (except the sweat glands) are innervated by the {{c1::parasympathetic::parasympathetic or sympathetic?}} nervous system

cards.back:
1. Mechanically --> **Chew** **food up** and break into smaller pieces.

2. Chemically --> **Enzymes** in saliva.
cards.front: In what way 2 ways does the mouth break down food?

cards.back:
Salivary amylase = **breaks down starch** into smaller sugars

Lipase = **breaks down lipids** via ***hydrolysis***

No protein digestion occurs in the mouth

Protects stomach lining from acidic damage

cards.back:

Pepsin digests proteins in the stomach

NOTE: ***H+ cleaves bonds b/w hydrophobic/aromatic AAs***

***

cards.front: Most enzymes are most active at a {{c1::neutral pH::low pH or neutral pH?}}

cards.back:
Optimal pH ≈ pH of native environment

Pepsin (**stomach**) → **pH ~2**

Trypsin (**small** **intestine**) → **pH ~8**

Salivary amylase (**mouth**) → **pH ~6.5**

Formed in the stomach and passed to the small intestine

Result of mechanical and chemical digestion in acidic conditions

cards.back:
Breaks food into smaller pieces

Improves efficiency of enzyme action and nutrient absorption

Break down trimers and dimers into absorbable monomers

**Essential for final steps of digestion**

cards.front: What are brush-border enzymes?

**Each targets specific substrates** (e.g. *disaccharides*, *peptides*)

Work together to complete digestion into absorbable monomers

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0HsW6LVdRQ4)
cards.front: How many brush border enzymes are there?

cards.back:
Triggers release of pancreatic juices into duodenum

**Raises GI tract pH by** ***inhibiting*** **parietal** **cells** and **increasing pancreatic bicarbonate**

Slows gastric motility to allow more time for nutrient absorption

Stimulates release of bile and pancreatic juices **into the small intestine**

Also promotes satiety through neural signaling

cards.front: What is the role of Cholecystokinin (CKK)?

cards.back:
Stores bile for later use

**Secretes bile into the small intestine** ***in response to CCK***

Aids in digestion of fats

**Emulsifies fats into smaller droplets**

Improves fat digestion and absorption in small intestine

made in liver

cards.front: What is Bile and what is its function?

cards.back:
Bile salts have hydrophobic and hydrophilic regions → **emulsify fats into small droplets**

Suspends fats in aqueous digestive fluids (**mechanical** **digestion**)

Improves access for ***pancreatic lipase*** to chemically break down fats

**Secreted into duodenum to neutralize acidic chyme** and aid digestion

cards.back:
1. Filtration

2. Secretion

3. Reabsorption
cards.front: What are three processes by which the Kidney filters the blood and maintains blood concentration and volume?

cards.back:
Filtration = **passive movement of small molecules from blood into Bowman’s capsule**

Driven by pressure differences (***Starling forces***) across glomerular pores

Allows **water and small solutes to enter nephron, blocks large molecules**

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2024.png)
cards.front: What is filtration?

cards.back:
Can pass: small molecules (**glucose**, **H2O**, **electrolytes**, **fatty** **acids**, **single** AAs

Cannot pass = large molecules (**cells**, **proteins**, **polypeptide** **chains**)
cards.front: What kinds of things can make it through the glomerular pores and what kinds of things can't?
Filtration is a {{c1::passive::active or passive}} process

cards.back:
Secretion = active or passive transport of waste **into the nephron**

Removes substances too large **to pass through glomerular pores**

Helps eliminate toxins, drugs, and excess ions from the blood

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2024.png)
cards.front: What is Secretion?

cards.back:
Depends on solute composition in blood

**Nephron adjusts function based on body’s current metabolic needs**

Ex. high protein diet → more ammonia → converted to urea in liver → increased urea secretion into urine
cards.front: What determines the activty of secretion and reabsorption in the nephron?

cards.back:
Reabsorption = process of moving useful solutes from filtrate back into blood

Recovers important molecules like **glucose**, **amino** **acids**, and **electrolytes**

Prevents loss of essential nutrients in urine

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2024.png)
cards.front: What is Reabsorption?

cards.back:
Keep what body needs (**sugars**, **amino** **acids**, sometimes **water** etc.)

Lose what the body doesn't need (**waste** products, sometimes **water**, etc.)
cards.front: What are the kidney's two main goals in filtering the blood?

cards.back:
PCT = site of major reabsorption and secretion

**Reabsorbs useful molecules into vasa recta (amino acids, glucose, vitamins, salts,** **water)**

Secretes waste products into filtrate (**H⁺,** **K⁺, urea, NH₃, etc.**)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/health-and-medicine/circulatory-system/blood-pressure-control/v/parts-of-a-nephron)
cards.front: What occurs in the Proximal Convoluted Tubule?

cards.back:
**H+**, **U**rea, **N**H3, and **K**+

MNEMONIC: **DUMP** the **HUNK**
cards.front: What are the major waste productes excreted in the urine?

cards.back:
Deeper in kidney --> interstitial [solute] increases

**Maintains osmotic balance w/ the nephron** (especially loop of Henle)

Prevents H2O from rushing unctrollably into/out nephron
cards.front: What happens as you get deeper into the kidney?

cards.back:
Interstitium = **space surrounding nephron**

Site of solute and water exchange **b/w nephron and kidney tissue**
cards.front: What is the interstitium?

cards.back:
**[Filtrate] varies along nephron**, but interstitium stays isotonic to its local region

*Concentrated* filtrate is matched by *concentrated* interstitium → prevents water from rushing in (bursting)

*Dilute* **filtrate** is matched by *dilute* **interstitium** → prevents water from rushing out (collapsing)

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m571.jpg)
cards.front: The concentration of the filtrate changes dramatically as it moves through the nephron. What prevents water from rushing into the nephron and bursting it when the filtrate is very concentrated, and what prevents water from rushing out of the nephrone and collapsing it when the filtrate is very dilute?

cards.back:
Isotonic = solution w/ same solute concentration as inside of cell or tubule

**No net water movement occurs** — water enters and exits at equal rates

Maintains fluid balance and prevents swelling or shrinking

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m39.jpg)
cards.front: What does it mean to be isotonic?

cards.back:
Hypotonic = **solution less concentrated than inside of cell or tubule**

Water moves into cell, following the higher solute concentration

Can cause cells to swell and potentially burst

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m39.jpg)
cards.front: What does it mean to be in a hypotonic solution?

cards.back:
Hypertonic = solution more concentrated than inside of cell or tubule

**Water moves out of cell **toward higher solute concentration

Causes cells to shrink and shrivel due to water loss

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m39.jpg)
cards.front: What does it mean to be Hypertonic?

cards.back:
Descending loop of Henle = **permeable only to water**

Interstitial [solute] increases into medulla --> **water flows out of filtrate**

Water is reabsorbed into the blood via vasa recta

**If body is well-hydrated, interstitial concentration decreases** →* less water is reabsorbed*

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m571.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/health-and-medicine/circulatory-system/blood-pressure-control/v/parts-of-a-nephron)
cards.front: What happens in the descending loop of Henle?

cards.back:
Ascending loop = permeable to salts, ***impermeable*** ***to water***

**Interstital concentration decreases** → salts flow out of the filtrate

Salt reabsorption helps dilute the filtrate and concentrate the interstitium

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m637.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/health-and-medicine/circulatory-system/blood-pressure-control/v/parts-of-a-nephron)
cards.front: What happens in the ascending loop of Henle?

cards.back:
Diluting segment = **thick upper portion of the ascending loop of Henle**

***Actively*** transports salts out of the filtrate (even against a concentration gradient)

***Not permeable to water*** → creates very dilute filtrate

Only part of nephron that can make filtrate more dilute than blood

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m637.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/health-and-medicine/circulatory-system/blood-pressure-control/v/parts-of-a-nephron)
cards.front: What is the Diluting Segment of the Nephron?

cards.back:
DCT = responds to aldosterone --> promotes Na+ reabsorption -->** increases water reabsorption**

Also a site of waste product secretion (like H⁺, K⁺, urea, NH₃) -** like the PCT**

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m637.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/health-and-medicine/circulatory-system/blood-pressure-control/v/parts-of-a-nephron)
cards.front: What happens in the Distal Convoluted Tubule?

cards.back:
Collecting Duct = final site for urine concentration adjustment

Permeability to water is regulated by aldosterone and ADH

More permeability → more water reabsorbed → concentrated urine

Less permeability → less water reabsorbed → dilute urine

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m637.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/health-and-medicine/circulatory-system/blood-pressure-control/v/parts-of-a-nephron)
cards.front: What happens in the Collecting Duct?

cards.back: Reabsorption is the movement of things from the urine to the blood. If water is moving from the urine into the blood, there is less water in the urine, i.e. more concentrated urine.
cards.front: As the permeability of the collecting duct increases, it is easier for water to be reabsorbed. This causes the urine to become {{c1::more::more or less concentrated?}}

cards.back:
Aldosterone inserts Na⁺/K⁺ pumps into the DCT membrane

**Pumps 3 Na⁺ out** (to blood), **2 K⁺ in **(from blood)

Water follows Na⁺ out → **more water reabsorbed**

*↑ blood volume & pressure, ↓ urine output*

*
*
[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/health-and-medicine/circulatory-system/blood-pressure-control/v/aldosterone-raises-blood-pressure-and-lowers-potassium)*
*
cards.front: What exactly does Aldosterone do to the DCT to exert its effects?

cards.back:
Mnemonic: **D**amnit Aldosterone

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/health-and-medicine/circulatory-system/blood-pressure-control/v/aldosterone-raises-blood-pressure-and-lowers-potassium)
cards.front: Aldosterone acts on the {{c1::DCT::DCT or PCT?}}

cards.back:
ADH inserts aquaporins into collecting duct membrane

**Increases water permeability of the duct**

More water reabsorbed into blood → *concentrated* *urine*, increased blood volume

NOTE: ADH Dilutes blood (just water reabsorbed)
Aldosterone does NOT (Na+ excreted, water follows)
cards.front: What exactly does ADH do to the collecting duct to exert its effects?

cards.back:
ADH = reabsorbs water ***alone*** from the collecting duct

↑ blood volume, ↓ blood osmolarity ***(dilutes blood)***

Aldosterone = reabsorbs Na⁺ from the DCT; **water follows**

↑ blood volume, maintains blood osmolarity (***no dilution***)
cards.front: How are the ways ADH and Aldosterone affect the reabsorption from the kidney different?

cards.back:
Kidneys regulate blood pH by secreting H⁺ or HCO₃⁻

**Shifts bicarbonate buffer equation to maintain pH balance**

Helps correct acidosis (*by excreting H⁺*) or alkalosis (*by excreting HCO₃⁻*)
cards.front: How do the kidneys affect the body's maintenance of blood pH?

cards.back:
Kidneys regulate how much water and salt are reabsorbed into the blood

More water reabsorbed → higher blood volume → higher blood pressure

Less water reabsorbed → lower blood volume → lower blood pressure

cards.back:
Salivary amylase (mouth)

– Starch → maltose

Sucrase (small intestine, produced by intestinal glands)

cards.front: What enzymes are important for cabohydrate digestion (Didn't memorize this card)

cards.back:
Pepsin (stomach, secreted as pepsinogen by chief cells of gastric glands)

– **Hydrolyzes peptide bonds** (esp. aromatic AAs like F, W, Y)

HCl (stomach, secreted by parietal cells of gastric glands)

– Activates **pepsinogen → pepsin**

Trypsin (small intestine, secreted as trypsinogen by pancreas)

– **Hydrolyzes peptide bonds, activates other proteases** (e.g., chymotrypsinogen → chymotrypsin)

Chymotrypsin (small intestine, secreted as chymotrypsinogen by pancreas)

– **Hydrolyzes peptide bonds** (*activated by trypsin*)

Carboxypeptidase (small intestine, produced by pancreas)

– **Hydrolyzes terminal peptide at carboxyl end** (*activated by trypsin*)

Aminopeptidase (small intestine, produced by intestinal glands)

– **Hydrolyzes terminal peptide at amino end**

Dipeptidases (small intestine, produced by intestinal glands)

– **Hydrolyzes pairs of amino acids**

Enterokinase (small intestine, produced by intestinal glands)

– Converts **trypsinogen → trypsin**

cards.back:
ACh → sarcolemma depol. → AP travels via T-tubules → SR releases Ca²⁺

Ca²⁺ binds troponin → tropomyosin shifts → myosin sites exposed

Globular heads of Myosin-ADP binds actin

ADP dissociates → power stroke → actin pulled toward M-line (shortening sarcomere)

New ATP binds myosin → detaches from actin

ATP → ADP + Pi → myosin recocks to uncontracted condition

Ca²⁺ removed → muscle relaxed, myosin-ADP ready again

Weaker contraction = recruit fewer muscle fibers

Signal is all-or-nothing, **but fiber recruitment varies**

cards.front: Which macromolecule is responsible for our genetics?

cards.back:
A manifestation of bacterial transformation (Chapt. 1)

Had two bacteria: one deadly, one harmless
Harmless → mice lived
Deadly → mice died

Heat-killed deadly bacteria → mice lived

Heat-killed deadly + harmless → mice died

Harmless bacteria picked up genetic info from deadly bacteria (via transformation)

Experiment showed a heritable substance that could transfer traits between bacteria

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/dna-as-the-genetic-material/dna-discovery-and-structure/a/classic-experiments-dna-as-the-genetic-material)
cards.front: What is Griffith's transforming principle experiment?

cards.back:
Repeated the transforming experiment under 2 new conditions

1) Experiment was done in presence of DNA-degrading enzymes --> No transformation was observed

2) Experiment was done in presence of **protein-degrading enzymes** --> **Transformation** was observed

Suggests that ***DNA***, not protein, ***was the transferrable genetic material***

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/dna-as-the-genetic-material/dna-discovery-and-structure/a/classic-experiments-dna-as-the-genetic-material)
cards.front: What did Avery, MacLeod, and McCarty do after they replicated Griffith's transforming experiment?

cards.back:
Knew viruses inject genetic material; protein coat stays outside

Labeled DNA with ³²P (**phosphorus in DNA**, not protein)

Labeled protein with ³⁵S (**sulfur** **in** **protein**, not DNA)

³²P was **found inside infected bacteria **→ DNA entered

³⁵S **stayed** **outside** → protein did not enter

Conclusion: ***DNA is the genetic material, not protein***

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/dna-as-the-genetic-material/dna-discovery-and-structure/a/classic-experiments-dna-as-the-genetic-material)

cards.front: What is a frameshift mutation?

cards.back:
Reading frame refers to the fact that DNA is translated into Amino Acids in a 3 to 1 relationship. That is to say, three DNA bases in a row will code for 1 Amino Acid. Therefore, a single addition or elimination of DNA will shift the entirety of the reading frame, resulting in a very different polypeptide.

cards.back:
Segment of DNA on chromosome is swapped with a segment of DNA on another chromosome.

cards.front: Describe a translocation chromosomal mutation?

cards.back:
No --> can be good or bad

Not necessarily. A mutation can lead to a new amino acid in a protein that alters its function. This can be bad if it makes the protein unable to serve its original function, but it can be good if it makes the protein better able to serve its original function. Or, the new protein may be unable to serve its original function, but it might be able to serve some new function now.

Mutation results in basically random effects, and although certain types of mutations are known to usually be more harmful, any given mutation could potentially be potential or maladaptive.
cards.front: Are mutations necessarily bad?

cards.back:
Class of deleterious mutations involving genes of metabolism

Children born w/ them require **early intervention to prevent permanent damage from metabolite build up**
cards.front: What are inborn errors of metabolism?

cards.back:
Flow of genes b/w species

Happens when 2 species make viable hybrid offspring

Ex. Cow + bison = beefalo which can reproduce w/ cows or bison

cards.front: What is genetic leakage?

cards.back:
Change in composition of gene pool due to chance

Different to natural selection --> which is response to environmental selectors

cards.front: What is genetic drift?

cards.back:
In small population, random events have greater effects

In large populations they just cancel each other out

cards.front: Genetic drift is more prevelant in {{c1::small populations::small or large populations?}}

cards.back:
Extreme case of genetic drift --> small pop finds itself in reproductive isolation b/c bottle necks that suddenly reduce population available for breeding

It's so named b/c small isolated pop. will take on characteristics of population that founded it

Note: b/c this is just extreme genetic drift, this phenomenon is predicated upon the randomness of evolution

cards.front: What is a punnet square?

cards.back:
Heterozygous genotypes have two different alleles on their two copies of a given chromosome, usually a dominant and a recessive allele

cards.front: What does it mean to be heterozygous in a genotype?

cards.back:
Homozygous genotypes have the same allele on both copies of their chromosomes.

The allele can be dominant or recessive, as long as they are the same.

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1391.jpg)

cards.front: What does it mean to be homozygous in a genotype?

cards.back:
The two alleles of one parent are placed on the vertical axis, and the two alleles of the other parent are placed on the horizontal axis.

Next, one goes from box to box filling them in with the parent's allele's. Each box is in a different row/column combination, so each box will have a specific genotype/phenotype.

Afterwards, the genotypes/phenotypes of the offspring are counted up and represented as a fraction or percentage chance of occuring.

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1348.gif)
cards.front: How are values assigned to the 4x4 punnet square?

cards.back:

cards.front: What is the P generation?

cards.back:

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1703.jpg)
cards.front: What is the F generation?

cards.back:
Special circumstance of punnet square where you solve for parent genotype

This is accomplished as follows.

An unknown parent is made to breed with a homozygous recessive parent.

The offspring are analyzed, and based off of the genotype and phenotype ratio, you can deduce the genotype of the unknown parent.

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1206.jpg)
cards.front: What is a test cross?

cards.back:
A dihybrid cross is just a punnet square, except that two different genes are being analyzed instead of just one. Since each gene has two alleles, there is a total of 4 alleles from both parents, and therefore 4x4=16 possible combinations of alleles.

cards.front: What is the hardy-weinberg principle?

cards.back:
Note: Really just 1 criteria --> no change in frequency of population alleles
This can be manifested in 5 dif ways

1. Large population (no genetic drift + alleles stay constnat)

2. No mutation that affect gene pool (alleles stay constant

3. Mating in population is random and not sexually selected

4. No migration if individuals into- or out-of the population (alleles stay constant)

5. Genes in population all equally successful at reproducing

As you can no doubt see, Hardy-Weinberg Equilibrium only applies to a theoretical population. However, although hardy-weinberg equilibrium is not perfect, the closer the real population is to the theoretical population, the more accurate the Hardy-Weinberg principles will prove to be.

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/her/heredity-and-genetics/v/hardy-weinberg)

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aax12eYKd4s)
cards.front: Describe Natural Selection.

cards.back:
1. Organisms produce offspring, very** few of which survive to reproductive maturity.**

2. Chance variations within individuals may be heritable. If the variation gives an organism a survival advantage of any sort, it is deemed favorable.

3. Individuals with more favorable variations are more likely to survive to reproductive age and produce offspring, thererby passing their genes into the next generation

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aax12eYKd4s)
cards.front: What are some basic tenets of Natural Selection theory?

cards.back:
Neo-Darwinism → modern update of Natural Selection

Adds mechanism for variation → genetic mutations → heritable changes in genome

Adds Inclusive Fitness → success of genes via group benefit, not just individual

Altruism example → harms individual fitness → boosts population’s reproductive success
cards.front: Describe Neo-Darwinism

cards.back:
Punctuated equilibrium → variation of Neo-Darwinism

Differs in timescale → evolution in short bursts, not gradual

Bursts = major shifts in selection pressure → rapid change → survivors stabilize until next shift

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Fik1u6O1Yc8)
cards.front: What is punctuated equilibrium?

cards.back:
1. Stabilizing Selection

2. Directional Selection

3. Disruptive Selection

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/her/heredity-and-genetics/a/natural-selection-in-populations)
cards.front: What are the three patterns of natural selection?

cards.back:
When population responds to selection pressure by stabilizing that gene in their population

Ex. human body has issues w/ being very short/very tall
So natural selection has selected for people within stable range of "normal heights"

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m432.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/her/heredity-and-genetics/a/natural-selection-in-populations)
cards.front: What is stabilizing selection?

cards.back:
Directional selection is when pressures in the environment select for a phenotype directly. For example, when all the fast animals can eat the leaves in the bushes, the tall giraffes that can reach the leaves in the trees don't starve to death and are able to pass their genes on. Overtime, this results in the absolute tallest giraffes of every generation having a lot of reproductive success, and giraffes evolving to be taller over time as a result.

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m213.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/her/heredity-and-genetics/a/natural-selection-in-populations)
cards.front: What is directional selection?

cards.back:
In Disruptive Selection, there are two different extremes that simultaneously adapt well to environmental pressure, and therefore those two different extremes are selected.

If these two extremes are selected for vigorously enough, their genetic information will become so different they can no longer successfully reproduce, thus resulting in the splitting of one species into two.
![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1036.png)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/her/heredity-and-genetics/a/natural-selection-in-populations)
cards.front: What is Disruptive Selection?

cards.back:
Adaptive radiation is when disruptive selection turns one species into two or more different species over time.

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m271.jpg)

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N7mLxvNTSog)

cards.front: What are the three patterns of evolution?

cards.back:
Divergent evolution refers to the independent development of dissimilar characteristics in two or more lineages sharing a common ancestor. E.g. some primate ancestor of ours diverging into a modern primate on one hand and us on the other.

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1224.png)

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=X-XtZyHcck4)
cards.front: What is Divergent Evolution?

cards.back:
Parallel Evolution refers to the process where related species with a common ancestor evolve in similar ways for a long period of time in response to similar environment pressures.

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2198.jpg)

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=D5llATiCgkI)
cards.front: What is Parallel Evolution?

cards.back:
Convergent evolution refers to the independent development of similar characteristics in two species that do not share a recent common ancestor.

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2573.jpg)

cards.front: What is a Transferase?

cards.back:
It's a mathematical representation of the cooperativeness of an enzyme.

If Hill's coefficient > 1:
Binding of one ligand **increases** **the** **affinity** of the enzyme for more ligands
*positive* *cooperative* binding is occuring.

If Hill's coefficient < 1:
Binding of one ligand **decreases** **the** **affinity** of the enzyme for more ligands
*negative cooperative* binding is occuring.

If Hill's coefficient = 1:
Binding of one ligand **does not affect** the affinity of the enzyme for more ligands
*no cooperation* is occuring.

cards.front: What is a vitamin?

cards.back:
Vitamin A (aka Carotene) is an unsaturated hydrocarbon associated with **vision**, **growth**, and **immune** **function**.

Vitamin A is converted to retinal for use in vision and retinoic acid for **gene** **expression** **during** the **growth** of epithelial tissues.

cards.front: What is Vitamin A?

cards.back:
Vitamin D (aka cholecalciferol) is a unsaturated hydrocarbon associated with **calcium** and **phosphate** **regulation**.

Vitamin D can be consumed or synthesized by the body using exposure to UV light.

In the **liver** and **kidneys**, Vitamin D is **converted to calcitriol**. Calcitriol increases calcium and phosphate uptake in the intestines.

The aromatic ring in vitamin E can capture free radicals safely, **protecting us from oxidative damage.**

cards.front: What are the main components of a DNA strand?

cards.back:
1. Two antiparallel DNA strands

2. Sugar-Phosphate backbone is on **outside** of helix, nitrogenous bases in the **middle**

3. Bases only pair w/ complementary bases **via H-bonds**

4. Specific pairing --> **# of A's = # of Ts**, and C's = G's

cards.back:
Grooves that **arise as a result of the double helix**

They are used as binding sites by regulatory proteins

Disrupt H-bonds holding bases together --> **separates the two DNA strands**

DNA strands brought back together after being denatured

cards.back:
DNA wrapped tightly around histones --> ***Transcriptionally silent*

RNA polymerase can't interact w/ heterochromatin** to make mRNA

Dark when viewed under microscope

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2321.jpg)

cards.front: What is Heterochromatin?

cards.back:
Euchromatin = DNA wrapped loosely around histones --> ***transcriptionally active*

RNA polymerase can interact w/ it to make mRNA**

Light when viewed under microscope

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/high-school-biology/hs-reproduction-and-cell-division/hs-chromosome-structure-and-numbers/v/chromosomes-chromatids-chromatin-etc)
cards.front: What is Euchromatin?

cards.back:
**C-G is stronger **--> has 3x H-bonds vs A-T's 2x

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2179.jpg)
cards.front: Which base pair is stronger, A-T or C-G?

cards.front: What is the replisome?

cards.back:
Where DNA starts to undwind during copying

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m329.jpg)
cards.front: What is the origin of replication?

cards.back: ![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2306.jpg)
cards.front: Generation of new DNA proceeds in {{c1::both directions::one direction or both directions?}}

cards.back:
Eukaryotes --> Multiple origins and result in 2x attached sister chromatids

**Prokaryotes** --> **One origin** and **result in** **2x** *unattached ***chromosomes**

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1199.jpg)
cards.front: How does replication of DNA proceed differently in prokaryotes versus eukaryotes?

cards.back:
Unwinds DNA --> **Generates 2x single stranded templates** ahead of the polymerase

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1425.jpg)

cards.front: What is the role of Helicase?

cards.back:
SSBs bind to unraveled DNA --> **Prevents reassociation of DNA** and **protects base pairs from enzymes**

cards.front: What is the role of single stranded DNA binding proteins?

cards.back:
Process of DNA wrapping on itself and getting tangled during replication

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2362.jpg)
cards.front: What is supercoiling?

cards.back:
Alleviates tension of DNA in front of helicase **so it doesn't supercoil/break

Temporarily cuts strands to relieve tension** then puts them back together
(*Breaks then repairs phosphodiester bonds in backbone*)

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2210.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/high-school-biology/hs-molecular-genetics/hs-rna-and-protein-synthesis/v/rna-transcription-and-translation)
cards.front: What is the role of topoisomerase?

cards.back:
Strands of** original DNA** that serve as template for replication

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2649.jpg)
cards.front: What is the parent strand?

cards.back:
The newly synthesized DNA strand

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1023.jpg)
cards.front: What is a daughter strand?

cards.back:
Each new strand has 1x parent strand (conserved) and** 1x daughter strand**

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1023.jpg)
cards.front: What does it mean when we say DNA replication is semiconservative?

cards.back:
Class of enzymes that reads the parent strand + **synthesizes daughter strand**

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/dna-as-the-genetic-material/dna-replication/a/molecular-mechanism-of-dna-replication)
cards.front: What is DNA polymerase?

cards.back:
**Reads parent DNA 3' to 5'** (weird!) but synthesizes daughter from 5' to 3'

Ensures daughter strand is antiparallel to parent strand

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1763.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/dna-as-the-genetic-material/dna-replication/a/molecular-mechanism-of-dna-replication)
cards.front: Describe the 5' to 3' directionality of DNA polymerase?

cards.back:
**Daughter strand that is copied continuously** because it's moving in same direction as replication fork

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m390.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/high-school-biology/hs-molecular-genetics/hs-rna-and-protein-synthesis/v/rna-transcription-and-translation)
cards.front: What is the leading strand?

cards.back:
Strand copied in direction opposite of the replication fork

Body has had to evolve Okazaki fragment approach to synthesize lag strand correctly

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1804.png)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/high-school-biology/hs-molecular-genetics/hs-rna-and-protein-synthesis/v/rna-transcription-and-translation)
cards.front: What is the lagging strand?

cards.back:
Short fragments of DNA that are discontinually produced **then joined together **

Makes the lagging strand

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1804.png)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/high-school-biology/hs-molecular-genetics/hs-rna-and-protein-synthesis/v/rna-transcription-and-translation)
cards.front: What are okazaki fragments?

cards.back:
1. **Helicase** unwinds the DNA

2. **SSBs** protect the free DNA

3. **Primase** synthesizes RNA primers to **attract DNA polymerase**

4. **DNA Polymerase** binds and synthesizes DNA

5. RNA primers are removed

6. **DNA** **Ligase** joins Okazaki Fragments

7. **Topoisomerase** reduces tension in the advancing coil

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/high-school-biology/hs-molecular-genetics/hs-rna-and-protein-synthesis/v/rna-transcription-and-translation)
cards.front: What are the 7 basic steps to DNA replication?

cards.back:
Put first primer down then synthesize DNA until its done

NOTE: primers shown in green.
![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m339.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/high-school-biology/hs-molecular-genetics/hs-rna-and-protein-synthesis/v/rna-transcription-and-translation)
cards.front: The leading strand requires {{c1::one::one or many primers?}}

cards.back:
Each fragment requires its own RNA primer so DNA polymerase can bind

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m438.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/high-school-biology/hs-molecular-genetics/hs-rna-and-protein-synthesis/v/rna-transcription-and-translation)
cards.front: The lagging strand requires {{c1::many primers::one or many primers?}}

cards.back:
Enzyme that lays down RNA primers for **DNA polymerase to bind to**

cards.front: What is Primase?

cards.back:
RNA primers are removed in prokaryotes by DNA ***polymerase I. ***
RNA primers are **removed in Eukaryotes by *RNase H***

***
***

cards.front: How are RNA primers removed in Prokaryotes versus Eukaryotes?

cards.back:
Enzyme that joins together fragments of unconnected DNA

Ex. Okazaki fragments!

cards.front: What is DNA ligase?

cards.back:
Prokaryotes use DNA polymerase III.

**Eukaryotes** use **DNA polymerase** ***α***, ***δ***, and ***ε***.
cards.front: How is the DNA polymerase in prokaryotes and eukaryotes different?

cards.back: Alpha, Beta, Gamma, Delta, and Epsilon.
cards.front: What are the 5 classic DNA polymerases in Eukaryotic cells?

cards.back:
Work together to synthesize both leading and lagging strands

***δ*** also **fills in gaps left behind when RNA primers are removed**
cards.front: What is the combined role of DNA pol Alpha, Delta, and Epsilon?

cards.back: Gamma replicates mitochondrial DNA
cards.front: What is the role of DNA polymerase γ?

cards.back: Important for DNA repair process

cards.back:
Assisted by PCNA to form the **sliding clamp trimer**

Clapm helps **strengthen interaction** b/w polymerase and template strand
cards.front: What is the combined role of DNA pol delta and epsilon?

cards.back:
1. DNA pol I

2. DNA Pol II

2. DNA Pol III

cards.back: ![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2601.jpg)
cards.front: In what ways are the enzymes for DNA Replication similar and different in Prokaryotes versus eukaryotes?

cards.back:
Oncogenes are pieces of DNA that, if damaged (mutated) cause cancer.

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1560.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](http://127.0.0.1:49338/%22https://www.khanacademy.org/test-prep/mcat/biomolecules/gene-control/v/oncogenes)
cards.front: What are oncogenes?

cards.back:
Most oncogenes are genes related to cell-cycle and division timing

Your eye colour gene on the other hand won't give you cancer if it mutates

[Khan Academy Link](http://127.0.0.1:49338/%22https://www.khanacademy.org/test-prep/mcat/biomolecules/gene-control/v/oncogenes)
cards.front: What type of genetic info is more likely to be an oncogene?

cards.back:
Genes that stop and slow tumor progression

They **may prevent mutations to DNA **in the first place, **fix them **after they happen, or **kill cancer cells**

When these genes are mutated, they lose their anti-tumor properties

[Khan Academy Link](http://127.0.0.1:49338/%22https://www.khanacademy.org/test-prep/mcat/biomolecules/gene-control/v/oncogenes)
cards.front: What are anti-oncogenes?

cards.back:
1. Proofreading

2. Mismatch Repair

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/test-prep/mcat/biomolecules/dna/v/dna-repair-1)
cards.front: What are the two main ways DNA polymerase prevents errors in replication?

cards.back:
**Incorrectly** paired bases have **unstable H-bonds**

Proofreading section of DNA polymerase detects these and removes the incorrect base

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m663.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/test-prep/mcat/biomolecules/dna/v/dna-repair-1)
cards.front: Describe how DNA polymerase proof-reads bases.

cards.back:
In G2 phase, **special enzymes check DNA** for errors and correct them

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m480.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/test-prep/mcat/biomolecules/dna/v/dna-repair-1)
cards.front: Describe Mismatch Repair

cards.back:
1. Nucleotide **Excision** Repair

2. Base **Excision** Repair

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/test-prep/mcat/biomolecules/dna/v/dna-repair-2)
cards.front: What are the two main repair mechanisms of mismatch repair?

cards.back:
Section of damaged DNA strand is completely cut out --> *Phosphodiester back bone included*

DNA polymerase fills gap using the** undamaged strand as template**

Fixed strand is **sealed w/ DNA ligase**

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1707.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/test-prep/mcat/biomolecules/dna/v/dna-repair-2)
cards.front: Describe Nucleotide Excision Repair?

cards.back:
Damaged base is detected and removed via glycosylase enzyme

Leaves behind an **empty backbone called an AP site**

AP endonuclease recognizes the empty backbone and **cuts it out**

DNA polymerase then synthesizes complementary strand using the undamaged strand

**DNA ligase seals** the reapired strand back into place

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1298.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/high-school-biology/hs-molecular-genetics/hs-discovery-and-structure-of-dna/a/dna-proofreading-and-repair)
cards.front: Describe Base Excision Repair?

cards.back:
AKA endonucleases: **recognize palindromic dsDNA** sequences and cut them

NOTE: The palindromes MUST be even numbers! Exclude any answers that are odd

They are *isolated from bacteria and used to cut DNA in the lab
*
Create sticky ends! Useful for recombinant DNA stuff

(Palindrome = same 5'-3' sequence on both strands, opposite directions)

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1679.jpg) ![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m868.png)
cards.front: What are restriction enzymes?

cards.back:
Vector is usually bacterial or viral plasmid that can be **transferred to host bacterium**

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2693.jpg)
cards.front: What is a vector in the context of DNA Biotechnology?

cards.back:
It's a vector that's been **modified w/ new DNA**

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1204.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/biotech-dna-technology/dna-cloning-tutorial/v/dna-cloning-and-recombinant-dna)
cards.front: What is a recombinant vector in the context of DNA Biotechnology?

cards.back:
Use specific restriction endonuclease to **cut out a part of the vector DNA**

Use ***same*** restriction endonuclease to **cut piece of DNA of interest out**

Because same endonuclease was used: Foreign DNA will fit in hole made into vector DNA

Mix foreign DNA fragment w/ vector, **mix in annealing conditions then treat with ligase**

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2021.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/biotech-dna-technology/dna-cloning-tutorial/v/dna-cloning-and-recombinant-dna)
cards.front: How do you make a recombinant vector?

cards.back:
Insert DNA of interest into recombinant vector to instert into bacteria

Bacteria will grow and **replicate its DNA including the vector**

By letting colony grow, you'll generate large quantities of your DNA

Can either kill bacteria and re-treat w/ the **endonucleases** to collect all the DNA the bacteria made for you
OR
Make them express the gene so you can collect all the protein that's made from the DNA
(This is how we make insulin, we grow it in bacteria!)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/biotech-dna-technology/dna-cloning-tutorial/v/dna-cloning-and-recombinant-dna)
cards.front: What is the point of making a recombinant plasmid vector?

cards.back:
Large collections of known DNA sequences that are **cloned into vectors for use in future studies**

They can be genomic or complementary
cards.front: What are DNA libraries?

cards.back:
Genomic library --> coding (Exon) and non-coding (intron) regions
This is preferred for *sequencing the entirety of an organism's genome*

**Complementary** library --> Made by** reverse-transcribing** processed mRNA (**only contain exons** of DNA)
Preferred for sequencing *specific genes to identify their function*
Only way t*o make transgenic animals express foreign genes*, since it has only coding regions.
cards.front: What is the difference between a Genomic Library and a Complementary (expression) Library?

cards.back:
Process of bringing 2x complementary base pair sequences together

Can be **DNA-DNA recognition** or **DNA-RNA recognition**

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m350.jpg)
cards.front: What is Hybridization?

cards.back:
Process used to produce millions of copies of DNA sequence *without using bacteria*

Must be done w/ dsDNA

**DNA of interest** is placed **in solution of nucleotides** -- **denatured** -- **replicated** w/ custom primers -- **cooled** back down

Each round of PCR doubles amount of DNA so it only takes a few rounds to have lots of DNA

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2551.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/high-school-biology/hs-molecular-genetics/hs-biotechnology/v/the-polymerase-chain-reaction-pcr)
cards.front: Describe PCR

cards.back:
**DNA is (-)** so it will migrate towards (+) anode of eletrolytic cell

Larger DNA migrates slower, just like in protein electrophoresis

Agarose is preferred gel for DNA gel electrophoresis

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/biotech-dna-technology/dna-sequencing-pcr-electrophoresis/v/gel-electrophoresis-dna)
cards.front: Describe Gel electrophoresis for DNA

cards.back:
Used to detect presence and quantity of various DNA strands in a sample

**DNA is cut by restriction enzymes in specific ways** then separated by gel electrophoresis

Separated fragments then transferred to a membrane and **exposed to a DNA probe**

Probe is radioactive ssDNA sequence ***visible under x-ray***

If sequence in DNA and probe match up they will hybridize and that band of DNA on membrane will be visible

Ankit: usually for 2000-4000bp

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m882.jpg)

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EoTq-Ql_Zzc)
cards.front: What is a southern blot?

cards.back:
Uses dideoxyribonucleotides to determine sequence of DNA segment
(ddATP, ddGTP, etc.)

***They don't have -OH at C3*** --> **end DNA replication** once incorporated into DNA

Eventually **sample is composed of fragments** that end in dd-nucleotide of interest

Separate the fragments based on what dd-nucleotide they end in

Use ***gel Electrophoresis*** to see how long chain was when dd-nucleotide was incorporated to determine base order

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1667.jpg)

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FvHRio1yyhQ)
cards.front: How does DNA sequencing work?

cards.back:
Therapy for genetic diseases involving replacing the mutated/inaccurate copies with normal copies

**Modified viruses usually deliver the working gene** into host DNA

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m194.jpg)
cards.front: What is gene therapy?

cards.back:
Mice that have a cloned gene inserted into their zygote or other embryonic stem cell

Means they** have the gene in *ALL* adult cells**

Transgenes usually carry genetic diseases so we can study effects of disease from early embryonic development and through adulthood

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2580.jpg)
cards.front: What are transgenic mice?

cards.back:
KO mouse has one of its genes removed as a zygote

**Lacks the gene completely as an adult**

Used to study importance and effects of different genes
cards.front: What is a knockout mouse?

cards.back: More H-bonds = more IMFs = higher denaturation temperature.
cards.front: The more GC pairs in a DNA strand the {{c1::higher::higher or lower}} the denaturation temperature
