cards.front: What is the central dogma of biology?

cards.back:
1. mRNA

2. tRNA

3. rRNA
cards.front: What are the three main types of RNA?

cards.back:
Any three nucleotides in a row

They're **what ribosomes read** **to** **translate** mRNA into AAs

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m51.jpg)
cards.front: What is a codon?

cards.back:
Link b/w DNA and proteins

DNA transcribed into mRNA which **travels out of nucleus to ribosomes**

Ribosomes translate them into proteins

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2365.jpg)
cards.front: What is mRNA?

cards.back:
Monocistronic RNA = mRNA can be translated into ***ONE*** protein product

This means **every single one of the proteins we contain has its own mRNA strand**

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Amfz59f87YU)
cards.front: What does it mean for eukaryotic mRNA to be monocistronic?

cards.back:
Polycistronic mRNA = mRNA can be translated into ***>1*** protein product

So 10 **different proteins in a bacteria may be from same mRNA**

Possible b/c you can get different protein if you don't translate all the mRNA or start at dif places

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m66.jpg)

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Amfz59f87YU)
cards.front: What does it mean for prokaryotic mRNA to be polycistronic?

cards.back:
tRNA translates language of nucleic acids into amino acids at the ribosome

Each tRNA contains** folded strand of RNA that includes 3-nucleotide anticodon** ***and an amino acid***

tRNA anticodon binds codon of mRNA --> brings with it the right AA

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m113.jpg)
cards.front: What is tRNA?

cards.back:
tRNA molecules **don't always have an AA attached**

Charged or activated tRNA = tRNA w/ an AA attached

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m97.jpg)
cards.front: What does it mean when someone says a tRNA molecule is charged or activated?

cards.back:
Class of enzymes that attach specific AAs to specific tRNA molecules
(Based on the anticodon)

**Each AA is activated by different **aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase

AAs are always added to the free -OH at the 3' end of tRNA

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m97.jpg)
cards.front: What is aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase?

cards.back:
Synthesized in the **nucleolus** --> an important structural component of ribosomes

rRNA can ***also act as ribozymes***

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1370.png)

cards.front: What is rRNA?

cards.back: A strand of RNA with enzymatic properties
cards.front: What is a ribozyme?

cards.back:

cards.front: What are the three stop codons?

cards.back:
AUG

Methionine

Mnemonic: School starts in **AUG**ust

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/gene-expression-central-dogma/central-dogma-transcription/a/the-genetic-code-discovery-and-properties)
cards.front: What is the start codon?

cards.back:
Start/Stop codons start and stop protein translation respectively

Start translating mRNA when it sees AUG

**Stop** **translation** when it sees **UAA**, **UGA**, or **UAG**

U Are Annoying
U Go Away
U Are Gone
![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1903.jpg)

cards.front: Describe start and stop codons

cards.back:
Process of protein synthesis in ribosome using an mRNA template

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m25.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/gene-expression-central-dogma/translation-polypeptides/v/translation-mrna-to-protein)
cards.front: What is translation?

cards.back:
They're specific b/c each one codes for ONE amino acid

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2151.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/high-school-biology/hs-molecular-genetics/hs-rna-and-protein-synthesis/a/the-genetic-code)
cards.front: What does it mean when we say codons are specific?

cards.back:
They're degenerate because multiple codons code for the same AA

This is most notably seen in third base wobble

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m120.png)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/high-school-biology/hs-molecular-genetics/hs-rna-and-protein-synthesis/a/the-genetic-code)
cards.front: What does it mean when we say codons are degenerate?

cards.back:
The tendency for the third base in a codon to not be as important in determining the AA

It's an evolutionary development **designed to protect from mutations**

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2348.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/gene-expression-central-dogma/translation-polypeptides/a/trna-and-ribosomes)
cards.front: What is third base wobble?

cards.back:
1. Silent Mutation

2. Missense Mutation

3. Nonsense Mutation

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.google.com/search?q=point+mutations+khan+academy&oq=Point+Mutations+khan+a&aqs=chrome.0.0j69i57.1377j0j9&sourceid=chrome&ie=UTF-8)
cards.front: What are the three types of point mutations?

cards.back:
When **3rd nucleotide of a codon is swapped** for another but no change in AA

Results in no change in the protein product

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2163.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.google.com/search?q=point+mutations+khan+academy&oq=Point+Mutations+khan+a&aqs=chrome.0.0j69i57.1377j0j9&sourceid=chrome&ie=UTF-8)
cards.front: What is a silent mutation?

cards.back:
An altered codon substitutes in a different amino acid

**Effect on protein product is variable** --> depends on how different the AA is/location/etc.

If new AA is not very different, then protein function less likely to be affected

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1048.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.google.com/search?q=point+mutations+khan+academy&oq=Point+Mutations+khan+a&aqs=chrome.0.0j69i57.1377j0j9&sourceid=chrome&ie=UTF-8)
cards.front: What is a missense mutation?

cards.back:
Mutation when altered codon = premature STOP codon

**Almost always lead to non-functional proteins**

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m734.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.google.com/search?q=point+mutations+khan+academy&oq=Point+Mutations+khan+a&aqs=chrome.0.0j69i57.1377j0j9&sourceid=chrome&ie=UTF-8)
cards.front: What is a nonsense mutation?

cards.back:
Refers to way the entire strand of DNA and RNA is framed in triplets (***codons***)

Reading frame is **crucial in understanding frameshift mutations**

By adding or substracting a base, you don't just affect that one base, you shift the ENTIRE reading frame.

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1617.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.google.com/search?q=point+mutations+khan+academy&oq=Point+Mutations+khan+a&aqs=chrome.0.0j69i57.1377j0j9&sourceid=chrome&ie=UTF-8)
cards.front: What is the reading frame?

cards.back:
Mutation that shifts entire reading frame of the genetic info

1. Frameshift **deletion** --> base is deleted and frame shifts ***down*** one base

2. Framsehift **Insertion** - a base is added and the frame shifts ***up*** one base.

Notice, *if three bases were removed at once, the frame would actually be conserved*
*
*

cards.front: What is a frameshift mutation and what are the two types?

cards.back: [Khan Academy Link](https://www.google.com/search?q=point+mutations+khan+academy&oq=Point+Mutations+khan+a&aqs=chrome.0.0j69i57.1377j0j9&sourceid=chrome&ie=UTF-8)

cards.back:
Process by which mRNA is synthesized by RNA polymerase from a strand of template DNA.

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m207.png)
cards.front: What is transcription?

cards.back:
Helicase needs to unwind DNA + Topoisomerase nicks strand to prevent super coiling

(**Just like in DNA replication**)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/high-school-biology/hs-molecular-genetics/hs-rna-and-protein-synthesis/v/rna-transcription-and-translation)
cards.front: What needs to happen before RNA pol can access DNA and transcribe it?

cards.back:
DNA strand that's read by RNA polymerase to create the mRNA

**Transcript bases will be antiparallel** and **complementary** to template strand

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1676.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/dna-as-the-genetic-material/dna-replication/a/molecular-mechanism-of-dna-replication)
cards.front: What is the template strand?

cards.back:
Coding strand = not read by RNA polymerase

Bases of the mRNA will be ***parallel*** and ***equivalent*** **to the bases in the coding strand** (U sub in for Ts tho)

Use coding strand to determine mRNA transcript of a DNA segment
--> Much easier!

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1676.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/dna-as-the-genetic-material/dna-replication/a/molecular-mechanism-of-dna-replication)
cards.front: What is the coding strand?

cards.back:
***No*** --> They search for specialized DNA regions (**promoter** **regions**) and only transcribes starting there

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1732.jpg)
cards.front: Does RNA polymerase just randomly transcribe segments of DNA as they open up?

cards.back:
1. RNA pol 1 - Located in **Nucleolus**, synthesizes **rRNA**.

2. ** **RNA** **pol 2** - **Located in the **nucleus**, **transcribes** **DNA** and **some snRNA**.
*This is the transcription RNA pol*

3. RNA pol 3 - Located in the **Nucleus**, **synthesizes** **tRNA** and **some rRNA**
cards.front: What are the three types of RNA pol in eukaryotes?

cards.back:
RNA polymerase binding site** within promoter region** in eukaryotic DNA

Able to be separated easily b/c of relative weakness of T-A bonds

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m346.png)
cards.front: What is the TATA box?

cards.back:
Proteins that bind DNA to help/prevent gene transcription

To help --> help RNA pol find + bind DNA of interest

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m346.png)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/ap-biology/gene-expression-and-regulation/regulation-of-gene-expression-and-cell-specialization/v/regulation-of-transcription)
cards.front: What are transcription factors?

cards.back:
RNA pol reads in the 3'->5' direction so that it **can synthesize nucleotides in the 5'->3' direction. **

Nucleotides are always synthesized in the 5' -> 3' direction!

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m654.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/gene-expression-central-dogma/transcription-of-dna-into-rna/v/transcription-and-mrna-processing)
cards.front: In what direction does RNA polymerase read and synthesize?

cards.back:
hnRNA = **heterogenous nuclear** RNA

hnRNA = mRNA transcript PRIOR to post-transcriptional modifications

B/c hnRNA hasn't been processed yet, it will be **a perfect RNA version of the DNA strand**

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1018.jpg)
cards.front: What is hnRNA?

cards.back:
Series of modifications made to hnRNA to make into mRNA.

Three most important post transcriptional processes are:
1. Intron/Exon Splicing
2. 5' Cap
3. 3' Poly-A tail

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2287.jpg)
cards.front: What is postranscriptional processing?

cards.back:
Process of cutting out non-coding (**introns**) and reconnecting the coding sequences (**exons**)

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1081.jpg)

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xZwSmUNRBQQ)
cards.front: Describe Splicing

cards.back:
Name for a lasso shaped structure.

Refers to the **way introns are spliced out** of the RNA transcript

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m858.jpg)
cards.front: What is a lariat?

cards.back:
Specialized complex handling splicing of RNA

Comprised of snRNA and small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs)

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1528.jpg)
cards.front: What is the spliceosome and what is it made of?

cards.back:
Evolutionary function of introns is not well understood

Hypothesized they play role in maintaining appropriate size of our genome **for regulating gene expression
**
Khan Academy Link
cards.front: Why do we even have introns? What is the point of chunks of rna that don't code for anything?

cards.back:
The 5' cap = methylated GTP molecule

**Protects mRNA from degradation** in the cytoplasm

Also recognized by ribosome as a binding site

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1551.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/ap-biology/gene-expression-and-regulation/transcription-and-rna-processing/v/post-translational-regulation)
cards.front: What is the purpose of the 5' Cap?

cards.back:
Depending on how hnRNA is spliced --> can get different proteins

Hypothesized to make it so we can fit more potential proteins into smaller amounts of DNA/RNA

Ex. same DNA segment and the hnRNA transcript could be spliced 5 ways to make 5 different proteins

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m521.jpg)

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=xZwSmUNRBQQ)
cards.front: What is meant by alternative splicing?

cards.back:
The 3' Poly A Tail is a long chain of Adenines.

Shield for mRNA transcript in the cytoplasm

As soon as **mRNA hits cytoplasm**, the **tail starts getting destroyed**

Longer poly-A tail = more time mRNA has to get translated

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2153.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/ap-biology/gene-expression-and-regulation/transcription-and-rna-processing/v/post-translational-regulation)
cards.front: What is the purpose of the 3' Poly- A tail?

cards.back:
UTR = untranslated region.

Refers to small portions at ends of RNA transcript that don't get translated

So UTR = mRNA before start codon and after stop codon
cards.front: What is a UTR?

cards.back:
Structure made of proteins and RNA that associates with mRNA in the cytoplasm

Constructs chains of amino acids using tRNA's. ![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m585.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/gene-expression-central-dogma/translation-polypeptides/v/translation-mrna-to-protein)
cards.front: What is the ribosome?

cards.back:
1. A - AminoAcyl Site

2. P - Peptidyl Site

3. E - Exit Site

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/gene-expression-central-dogma/translation-polypeptides/a/trna-and-ribosomes)
cards.front: What are the three binding sites for tRNA's in ribosomes?

cards.back:
1. Initiation

2. Elongation

3. Termination

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/gene-expression-central-dogma/translation-polypeptides/v/translation-mrna-to-protein)
cards.front: What are the three main steps of translation?

cards.back:
1. Initiation - Initiation Factors and **GTP**

2. Elongation- Elongation Factors and **GTP**

3. Termination - Releases Factors and **GTP**
**
**
[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/gene-expression-central-dogma/translation-polypeptides/v/translation-mrna-to-protein)**
**
cards.front: What are the necessary requirements for each step of translation?

cards.back:
The Shine-Dalgarno sequence is **seen in prokaryotes**

It's a piece of RNA in 5' UTR ***allowing the small subunit of ribosome to bind***

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1789.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/ap-biology/gene-expression-and-regulation/translation/v/differences-in-translation-between-prokaryotes-and-eukaryotes)
cards.front: What is the Shine-Dalgarno sequence?

cards.back:
Eukaryotes use 5' cap to recruit small subunit of the ribosome

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/ap-biology/gene-expression-and-regulation/translation/v/differences-in-translation-between-prokaryotes-and-eukaryotes)
cards.front: If prokaryotes use the Shine-Dalgarno sequence to recruit the small sub unit of the ribosome, how do eukaryotes do it?

cards.back:
1) Small ribosomal subunit **binds mRNA** (via *Shine*-*Dalgarno* in prokaryotes and *5-cap* in eukaryotes)

2) Activated initiator tRNA **binds start codon** via **base-pairing at P site of ribosome**

3) Large subunit binds small subunit w/ help of initiation factors --> forms completed initiation complex

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1741.jpeg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/gene-expression-central-dogma/central-dogma-transcription/a/the-genetic-code-discovery-and-properties)
cards.front: Describe Initiation

cards.back:
The A site holds incoming aminoacyl-tRNA.

This is the **next amino acid that is being added** to the growing chain.

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m407.gif)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/gene-expression-central-dogma/translation-polypeptides/a/trna-and-ribosomes)
cards.front: Describe the role of the A site

cards.back:
P site holds tRNA that carries the growing polypeptide chain

Also **where methionine (start AA) binds** during initiation

In this part of ribosome, peptidyl transferase uses GTP to transfer peptide chain **from tRNA in P site** **to tRNA of A site**

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m407.gif)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/gene-expression-central-dogma/translation-polypeptides/a/trna-and-ribosomes)
cards.front: Describe the role of the P site?

cards.back:
After tRNA in P site loses peptide chain, it's transferred to E site

Here it pauses for a sec before dissociating back into solution to recharge

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m407.gif)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/gene-expression-central-dogma/translation-polypeptides/a/trna-and-ribosomes)
cards.front: Describe the role of the E site.

cards.back:
Proteins that speed up elongation by **bringing in tRNAs and GTP**

Also get rid of GDP (used up GTP) so fresh GTP's can take their place.

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1980.gif)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/gene-expression-central-dogma/translation-polypeptides/v/translation-mrna-to-protein)
cards.front: What are Elongation Factors?

cards.back:
Part of mRNA that directs ribosome to move to RER and **finish translation there

*Meant for proteins that won't be in cytoplasm ***

Ex. secretory, membrane, and lysosomal proteins
cards.front: What is a signal sequence?

cards.back:
tRNA w/ correct AA enters A-site of ribosome

GTP used → polypeptide transferred from P-site tRNA → A-site tRNA

GTP used → ribosome shifts the tRNAs down (A→P site, P → E site)

tRNA exits E-site, next tRNA enters A-site

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m407.gif)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/gene-expression-central-dogma/translation-polypeptides/v/translation-mrna-to-protein)
cards.front: Describe Elongation.

cards.back:
When STOP codon moves to A site --> Release factor (a protein) binds the codon

Causes peptide to be hydrolyzed + released from tRNA

Ribosome then dissociates

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1680.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/gene-expression-central-dogma/translation-polypeptides/v/translation-mrna-to-protein)
cards.front: Describe Termination?

cards.back:
Post-Translational processing refers to any modifications made to a protein after it has already been translated.

1. Phosphorylation
2. Carboxylation
3. Glycosylation
4. Prenylation
cards.front: What is post-translational processing and what are the commom types?

cards.back:
Phosphorylation is used to activate or deactivate proteins, especially enzymes.

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1600.jpg)
cards.front: Generally speaking, how does phosphorylation affect proteins?

cards.back:
Done so protein can have Ca2+ binding sites

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m197.jpg)
cards.front: Generally speaking, how does carboxylation affect proteins?

cards.back:
Usually **done in the ER and golgi**

Used as a signal for where the protein is supposed to end in the cell

Ex. May take protein to lysosome or target to mito etc.

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m417.png)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/test-prep/mcat/biomolecules/dna/v/protein-modifications)
cards.front: Generally speaking, how does glycosylation affect proteins?

cards.back:
Addition of lipid groups

Done to membrane bound enzymes to they **associate w/ membrane well**

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m394.jpg)
cards.front: Generally speaking, how does prenylation affect proteins?

cards.back:
Operons

cards.front: What is the main way that prokaryotes regulate how much of their genome they are expressing?

cards.back:

2. Enhancers

cards.front: What are the 5 main ways that Eukaryotes regulate how much of their genome they are expressing?

cards.back:
Cluster of **genes transcribed into a single mRNA**

Contains Regulator Gene, Promoter Site, Operator Site, Structural Gene

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2640.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/gene-regulation/gene-regulation-in-bacteria/v/operons-and-gene-regulation-in-bacteria)
cards.front: Describe the structure of an operon?

cards.back:
An operon is like an on/off switch for certain genes in the ***prokaryotic chromosome.***

1. **Inducible** Systems

2. **Repressible** Systems

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/gene-regulation/gene-regulation-in-bacteria/v/operons-and-gene-regulation-in-bacteria)
cards.front: What is an operon and what are the two types?

cards.back:
Always-present repressor is bound to the operator --> stops RNA polymerase from transcribing
(Repressor is coded for by regulator)

If **inducer is present --> binds repressor**, allowing operon to be transcribed

Useful b/c **ties expression to presence of specific molecules**

Classic inducible system is the Lac Operon --> allows ***bacteria*** to **digest lactose when it's in high enough [ ] **

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1736.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/gene-regulation/gene-regulation-in-bacteria/v/operons-and-gene-regulation-in-bacteria)
cards.front: Describe an Inducible System operon?

cards.back:
Binding of a molecule reduces transcriptional activity

Ex. Repressor Proteins

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KXOvPVc6zeE)
cards.front: What is a negative control mechanism?

cards.back:
Molecule binding increases transcriptional activity

Ex. Inducer molecules

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ZHTqxczEY6Y)
cards.front: What is a positive control mechanism?

cards.back:
Molecule that binds repressor to remove it from the operon

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m154.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/gene-regulation/gene-regulation-in-bacteria/a/the-lac-operon)
cards.front: What is an inducer?

cards.back:
Always-present repressor protein cannot bind operator on it's own --> **RNA pol can transcribe gene**
(Repressor coded for by regulator)

If **co-repressor is present** --> binds repressor and complex represses the gene

Ties transcription to presence of specific molecule

Classic repressible system is the TRP operon -->** allows bacteria to synthesize TRP when it's low in the cell**
![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2084.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/gene-regulation/gene-regulation-in-bacteria/v/operons-and-gene-regulation-in-bacteria)
cards.front: Describe a Repressible System operon

cards.back:
Group of TFs that bind elements far from gene to **enhance it's transcription**

Large distance = DNA bending to bring the two regions close together

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1543.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/ap-biology/gene-expression-and-regulation/regulation-of-gene-expression-and-cell-specialization/v/regulation-of-transcription)
cards.front: What is an enhancer?

cards.back:
Certain cells modify genome and add more copies of a gene

**More** **copies** = more expression of protein

Ex. Skin cell have more copies of keratin expressing gene

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wEKQ1gQxR88)
cards.front: What is Gene Duplication?

cards.back:
They're **studded w/ (+) lysine residues**

They bind tightly to (-) phosphate backbone of DNA
cards.front: How exactly do histones get DNA to wrap so tightly?

cards.back:
(+) **lysine residues are acetylated** --> reduces their (+) charge

**Weakens binding of histone w/ DNA** --> Makes DNA looser and more easily transcribed

***M***ethylation = ***M***uted
Inc. (-) charge on DNA

***A***cetylation = ***A***ctive
Neutralizes K residues

![](https://www.researchgate.net/publication/236934361/figure/fig2/AS:202498271911937@1425290758359/Histone-acetylation-and-deactylation-Histone-acetyltransferase-HATs-adds-acetyl-groups.png)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/ap-biology/gene-expression-and-regulation/regulation-of-gene-expression-and-cell-specialization/v/dna-and-chromatin-regulation)
cards.front: What is Histone Acetylation?

cards.back:
***C*** and ***A*** nucleotides are methylated

Methyl groups **carry e- density in their bonds** --> inc. (-) charge of DNA

Strengthens interaction b/w histones + DNA -->** DNA is harder to transcribe

*M***ethylation = ***M***uted
Inc. (-) charge on DNA

***A***cetylation = ***A***ctive
Neutralizes K residues

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/ap-biology/gene-expression-and-regulation/regulation-of-gene-expression-and-cell-specialization/v/dna-and-chromatin-regulation)
cards.front: What is DNA methylation?

cards.back:
Special protein that wraps around newly synthesized proteins

**Protects** them and **changes microenvironment** in which the protein folds

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2269.jpg)
cards.front: What are chaperones?

cards.back:
1. **RNA** has **Ribose**, DNA has Deoxyribose

2. **RNA** has **Uracil**, DNA has Thymine

3. **RNA** is **single** **stranded**, DNA is double stranded. (*except in viruses!*)
cards.front: What are the main three differences between DNA and RNA?

cards.back:
Enhancers are more than 25 base pairs away from the transcription site.

**Promoters are within 25 base pairs** of the transcription site.

cards.back:
States the plasma membrane is mostly fluid membrane

It is studded and held together by proteins, cholesterols, and other groups

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1839.jpg)

cards.front: Describe the fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane.

cards.back:
Refers to sugar molecules attached to exterior of membrane

The glycoprotein coat is important for **cell** **recognition**, **signalling**, etc.

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2791.jpg)
cards.front: What is the glycoprotein coat?

cards.back:
Selectively regulate traffic into / out cell

Ex. chemical traffic through channel proteins or signal traffic through receptors
cards.front: What is the main purpose of the membrane?

cards.back:
They're always in flux and moving around

Constantly **rotating** and travelling **laterally** through membrane - they **can** **also** **flip** but this is less common

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2473.jpg)
cards.front: Describe the diffusion of phospholipids in the membrane

cards.back:
Collection of similar lipids (usually sphingolipids and cholesterols)

Can also be with **associated proteins that serve as attachment points for other molecules**

Often serve roles in signalling

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2387.jpg)

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=t9MG6_2d2EY)
cards.front: What is a lipid raft?

cards.back:
Specialized enzyme that helps phospholipids flip across the plasma membrane

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2457.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/test-prep/mcat/cells/cell-membrane-overview/v/membrane-dynamics)
cards.front: What is a flippase?

cards.back:
Generally **they can't stack well** --> decreases their IMFs

So unsaturated FAs ***decrease*** **membrane** **regidity** --> makes it more flexible/fluid

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m815.jpg)

cards.back:
Generally **stack** **well** --> increases their IMFs

So they ***increase*** **membrane** **rigidity** --> less flexible/fluid!

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2121.jpg)

Micelles = single-layered phospholipid vesicle

**Liposomes** = **double** layered phospholipid vesicle

cards.back:
Protein that completely passes through the bilayer.

cards.front: What is a transmembrane protein?

cards.back:
Protein that is **in the bilayer**, but only associates with the interior or exterior side of it.

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1171.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/ap-biology/cell-structure-and-function/plasma-membranes/v/cell-membrane-proteins)
cards.front: What is an embedded protein?

cards.back:
Protein that associates with the inside of the plasma membrane

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2238.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/ap-biology/cell-structure-and-function/plasma-membranes/v/cell-membrane-proteins)
cards.front: What is an integral protein?

cards.back:
Protein that associates w/ periphery of plasma membrane, often **binding** **to** **lipid** **rafts** or **integral** **proteins**.

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2238.jpg)
cards.front: What is a peripheral protein?

cards.back:
Allow for direct cell-cell communication + often found in bunches together

Also called **connexons** --> composed of 6 connexin molecules

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1100.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/test-prep/mcat/cells/cell-cell-interactions/v/cell-junctions)
cards.front: What is the role of gap junctions in the plasma membrane?

cards.back:
Prevent solutes from leaking into the space b/w cells by forming a **tight seal between cells.**

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1372.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/test-prep/mcat/cells/cell-cell-interactions/v/cell-junctions)
cards.front: What is the role of tight junctions in the plasma membrane?

cards.back:
**Bind adjacent cells by anchoring their cytoskeletions** together

Associated with intermediate filaments within the cells

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1778.jpg)

cards.front: What is the role of desmosomes in the plasma membrane?

cards.back:
Primary active transport is when an ATP molecule is used to directly power movement of molecules across a membrane.
**Secondary** **active** **transport** is when the** release of energy of one molecule going down its concentration gradient is used** to drive another molecule against its concentration gradient.
cards.front: What is the difference between primary active transport and secondary active transport?

cards.back:
1. Symporters

2. Antiporters

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/test-prep/mcat/cells/transport-across-a-cell-membrane/v/how-do-things-move-across-a-cell-membrane)
cards.front: What are the two types of secondary active transport?

cards.back:
Secondary active transport system that pushes both molecules in the same direction

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m869.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/test-prep/mcat/cells/transport-across-a-cell-membrane/v/how-do-things-move-across-a-cell-membrane)
cards.front: What is a symporter?

cards.back:
An antiporter is an active transport system that pushes molecules in opposite directions

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m869.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/test-prep/mcat/cells/transport-across-a-cell-membrane/v/how-do-things-move-across-a-cell-membrane)
cards.front: What is an antiporter?

cards.back:
Endocytosis is when the cell membrane invaginates and engulgs material to bring it into the cell.

1. Pinocytosis is endocytosis of fluid

2. **Phagocytosis** is the endocytosis of **solids**.

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2742.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/science/biology/membranes-and-transport/bulk-transport/v/endocytosis-phagocytosis-and-pinocytosis)

cards.back:
Membrane receptors binding appropropriate molecules = endocytosis

cards.back:
1. Sodium, Potassium, and Chloride leak channels

2.** Na+/K+ Pump**
cards.front: What are the main contributors to the resting membrane potential across any given cell membrane?

cards.back:
Highly permeable due to many large pores --> allow **passage** **of** **ions** and **small** **proteins**

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/test-prep/mcat/cells/eukaryotic-cells/v/mitochondria)
cards.front: Describe the outer membrane of the mitochondria

cards.back:
Selectively permeable membrane with **cristae** and **important metabolic enzymes
**

cards.front: Describe the inner mitochondrial membrane.

Move through cell layers by going through space ***between them***

decks.name: Captain Hook MCAT::2 - Biological and Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems::B) Biochemistry::09 Carbohydrate Metabolism I

cards.back:
Glut 2 and Glut 4

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i9S5_KZa_Is)
cards.front: What are the primary receptors responsible for transport of glucose into and out of cells?

cards.back:
Glut 2 is a low affinity glucose transporter found in **hepatocytes** (liver cells) and **pancreatic** **cells**.

The low affinity of this transporter allows it to only shuttle glucose into the liver and pancreas ***when glucose levels are high*** (like after a meal)

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i9S5_KZa_Is)
cards.front: Describe Glut 2

cards.back:
Glut 4 is a glucose transporter found in **adipose tissue** (fat) and **muscle**.

The rate of glucose transport for these tissues is ***increased by insulin.***

Insulin stimulates the production of more Glut4 receptors to line the membrane

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m13.jpg)

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i9S5_KZa_Is)
cards.front: Describe Glut 4
In muscles, excess glucose is converted into {{c1::glycogen::glycogen or DHAP?}}

cards.back: DHAP is ***converted into Glyercol Phosphate*** to store incoming fatty acids at triacylglycerols.
cards.front: In adipocytes, excess glucose is converted into {{c1::DHAP::glycogen or DHAP?}}

cards.back:
Cytoplasmic pathway that converts glucose into two pyruvate molecules, **releasing** a **modest amount of energy.
**
[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8qij1m7XUhk)
cards.front: What is glycolysis?

cards.back:
**1x ATP** used by **Hexokinase** to phosphorylate glucose to glucose-6-phosphate

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1807.jpg)

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8qij1m7XUhk)
cards.front: What is the first step of Glycolysis?

cards.back:
**Isomerase** isomerizes G6P to Fructose-6-P.

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1807.jpg)

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8qij1m7XUhk)
cards.front: What is the second step of Glycolysis?

cards.back:
**1x ATP** used by **PFK-1** to phosphorylate F6P to Fructose 1,6-bisphosphate

phosphfructokinase

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1807.jpg)

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8qij1m7XUhk)
cards.front: What is the third step of Glycolysis?

cards.back:
**Aldolase **cleaves **Fructose 1,6-bis P **into Glyceraldehyde-3-P** **and DHAP
(Dihydroxyacetone P)

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1807.jpg)

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8qij1m7XUhk)
cards.front: What is the 4th step of Glycolysis?

cards.back:
**DHAP** molecule converted into Glyceraldehyde 3-P by an **Isomerase** --> ***Makes 2 total GA3Ps***

Note: GA3P is only molecule that can continue down glycolytic pathway

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1807.jpg)

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8qij1m7XUhk)
cards.front: What is the 5th step of Glycolysis?

cards.back:
**GA3P Dehydrogenase** uses 2x phosphates + 2x NAD+

This ***oxidizes*** ***2x*** GA3P --> 1,3-Bisphosphoglycerate

This ***produces 2x NADH***

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1807.jpg)

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8qij1m7XUhk)
cards.front: What is the 6th step of Glycolysis?

cards.back:
**Phosphoglycerate Kinase** ***uses 2x ADP*** --> Converts ***2x*** 1,3-Bisphosphoglycerates into ***2x*** 3-Phosphoglycerates

***Generates 2x ATPs***

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1807.jpg)

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8qij1m7XUhk)
cards.front: What is the 7th step of Glycolysis?

cards.back:
**Mutase** converts ***2x*** 3-Phosphoglycerates into ***2x*** 2-Phosphoglycerates.

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1807.jpg)

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8qij1m7XUhk)
cards.front: What is the 8th step of Glycolysis?

cards.back:
**Enolase** converts ***2x* **2-Phosphoglycerates into ***2x* **Phosphoenolpyruvates **(PEP)**
**
**
![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1807.jpg)

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8qij1m7XUhk)
cards.front: What is the 9th step of Glycolysis?

cards.back:
**Pyruvate Kinase **uses ***2x* ADPs** to convert ***2x*** PEPs** **into ***2x* **Pyruvates and ***2x* **ATPs

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1807.jpg)

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8qij1m7XUhk)
cards.front: What is the 10th step of Glycolysis?

cards.back:
*2* ADP + *2* ATP + *2* NAD+ + Glucose -> *4* **ATP** + *2* **NADH** + *2* **Pyruvates**

There are also some hydrogen ions and water molecules but they aren't as important.

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8qij1m7XUhk)
cards.front: What is the overall metabolic reaction of Glycolysis?

cards.back:
Investment phase refers to consumption of ATP in steps 1 and 3 of Glycoylsis.

At this point, the **cell has actually made an energy investment** to metabolize glucose.

Investment pays off later when ATP is released by substrate level phosphorylation.

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1807.jpg)

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8qij1m7XUhk)
cards.front: What is the investment phase of glycolysis?

cards.back:
AMP is like ATP, but instead of three phosphates there is only one.

AMP acts as a "low energy" signal and will affect enzymes in the glycolytic pathway accordingly.

For this reason, **expect AMP to *activate* things that produce energy** and ***inactivate*** **things that consume it.**
cards.front: What is AMP and what is its general signalling function?

cards.back:
Hexokinase is present in most tissues and **phosphorylates 6 carbon sugars. **
It is a ***high** affinity enzyme* (low km).
Glucokinase is present only in* hepatocytes* and *pancreatic* *cells* and only phosphorylates glucose.
It is a ***low*** *affinity* *enzyme* (high km).

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2623.jpg)

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OG4A3Fkitvw)
cards.front: What is the difference between Hexokinase and Glucokinase?

cards.back:
In a series of reactions, one of them will be slower than the rest and therefore act as a bottleneck.

The rate limiting enzyme is the enzyme associated with the rate limiting step.
cards.front: What is a rate limiting enzyme?

cards.back:
***Step 3***, the conversion of Fructose 6-P** **into Fructose 1,6-bis P by **Phosphofructokinase-1
**
[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8qij1m7XUhk)
cards.front: What is the rate limiting step of Glycolysis?

cards.back:
PFK-1 is subject to negative feedback in the form of **inhibition by ATP and Citrate**.
This makes sense, because if you have a lot of energy and metabolic products (citrate), you can turn glycolysis off.

PFK-1 is also subject to ***activation*** by AMP.
This makes sense because if you have low energy (high AMP), you can turn glycolysis on.

Comes from β-oxidation of fatty acids, *not glycolysis.
*

Fatty acid–derived acetyl-CoA enables gluconeogenesis to **run efficiently using stored energy.**

decks.name: Captain Hook MCAT::2 - Biological and Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems::B) Biochemistry::10 Carbohydrate Metabolism II: Aerobic Respiration

cards.back:
AKA Krebs Cycle is series of metabolic reactions that occurs in the mitochondria.

The main function of this cycle is to **produce high-energy electron carriers** (NADH + FADH2) **by oxidizing Acetyl-CoA to CO2 and H2O.

** ![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1182.jpg)
cards.front: What is the citric acid cycle?

cards.back:
Contains high-energy thioester bond that can be used to **drive a multitude of other reactions** ***when hydrolysis occurs.***

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2177.png)
cards.front: What about Acetyl-CoA makes it such an archetypal metabolic molecule?

cards.back:
Enzyme complex in the mitochondrial matrix that produces acetyl-CoA and NADH.

PDH is **also inhibited by acetyl-CoA and NADH. **

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m540.jpg)

It is comprised of the following 5 enzymes.

1. Pyruvate Dehydrogenase
2. Dihydrolipoyl transacetylase
3. Dihydrolipoyl dehydrogenase
4. Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Kinase
5. Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Phosphatase
cards.front: What is Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Complex and what are its 5 components?

cards.back:
Pyruvate Dehydrogenase oxidizes pyruvate, **creating CO2**.

It requires Thiamine and Mg2+ to function.

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m540.jpg)
cards.front: What is Pyruvate Dehydrogenase's role in the PDH complex?

cards.back:
After pyruvate is oxidized, Dihydrolipoyl transacetylase oxidizes the remaining two-carbon molecule **using lipoic acid** and

Transfers the resulting acetyl group to CoA, forming Acetyl-CoA.

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m540.jpg)
cards.front: What is Dihydrolipoyl Transacetylase's role in the PDH complex?

cards.back:
Dihydrolipoyl Dehydrogenase uses FAD to reoxidize lipoic acid so it can be used again.

Doing so forms FADH2, which can **trade hydrogens with an NAD+ later** down the road to form NADH. ![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m540.jpg)
cards.front: What is Dihydrolipoyl Dehydrogenase's role in the PDH complex?

cards.back: Phosphorylates PDH **when ATP** or **acetyl**-**CoA** **levels are high**, ***which turns it off.***
cards.front: What is Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Kinase's role in the PDH Complex?

cards.back: Dephosphorylates PDH when **ADP levels are high,** ***which turns it on.***
cards.front: What is Pyruvate Dehydrogenase Phosphatase's role in the PDH complex?

cards.back:
1. CoA is coupled with a fatty acid (acyl group) in the cytoplasm.

2. **Acyl** **group** is transferred to carnitine to form acyl-carnitine, which **crosses the inner membrane of the mitochondria.**

3. Acyl group then transferred to a mitochondrial CoA to **reform the CoA-fatty acid **--> undergoes β-oxidation in mitochondria to form acetyl-CoA.

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1957.jpg)
cards.front: How do fatty acids (in the cytoplasm) increase the levels of Acetyl-Coa in the mitochondria?

cards.back:
1. Amino Acids can be broken into ketone bodies, which can be **turned into acetyl-CoA**

2. Ketone bodies can be converted to Acetyl-CoA **using the reverse reaction of the PDH complex.**

3. Alcohol can be converted into acetyl-CoA by **alcohol** **dehydrogenase** and **acetaldehyde** **dehydrogenase**.
cards.front: Other than fatty acids, how can the concentration of Acetyl-CoA be increased in the cell?

cards.back:
So, the citric acid cycle doesn't technically use Oxygen,
***
but*** it **won't occur without the presence of oxygen due to NADH build up, so it is considered aerobic.**
cards.front: The citric acid cycle is {{c1::aerobic::anaerobic or aerobic?}}

cards.back: ![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1482.jpg)

cards.back:
Acetyl-CoA and Oxaloacetate undergo **condensation** to form Citrate and free CoA

Catalyzed by Citrate Synthase

α-Ketoglutarate is oxidized to Succinyl-CoA by **a-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex**

Liberates an NADH and a CO2

This GTP will transfer its phosphate to ADP to form **ATP**.

This is the *only step that results in substrate level phosphorylation*

Succinate is converted into Fumarate by **Succinate Dehydrogenase**,

Also yields FADH2 from FAD

Unique step b/c *doesn't occur in mitochondrial matrix* --> Occurs within the inner membrane
**Succinate dehydrogenase is an integral protein on inner mitochondrial membrane**

cards.front: What are the three main control points of the citric acid cycle?

cards.back:
ATP and NADH (energy products) function as **allosteric inhibitors of Citrate Synthase. **

Succinyl-CoA and citrate are **also negative feedback **

If you already have energy products, why bother running Kreb's to make more?

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1727.jpg)

cards.front: Describe the regulation of Citrate Synthase

cards.back:
ATP and NADH (*energy products*) are **allosteric inhibitors of Isocitrate Dehydrogenase

ADP and NAD+** on the other hand (*low-energy signals*) activate Isocitrate Dehydrogenase.

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1727.jpg)

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ubzw64PQPqM)
cards.front: Describe the regulation of Isocitrate Dehydrogenase.

cards.back:
ATP NADH and Succinyl-CoA (energy products) **inhibit** **α-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase complex**

ADP and calcium ions stimulate it.

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1727.jpg)
cards.front: Describe the regulation of a-Ketoglutarate Dehydrogenase Complex

cards.back:
Series of enzymes in inner membrane of mitochondria that **use high energy electron carriers **(NADH and FADH2) to **generate ATP
**
[YouTube Link](https://youtu.be/C8VHyezOJD4)
cards.front: What is the electron transport chain?

cards.back:
Refers to electrochemical gradient of H+ from intermembrane space into matrix

The **force is used to generate ATP from ADP's and P's.** ![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1211.jpg)

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E_UG3WnsW3o)
cards.front: What is the proton motive force?

cards.back:
Their electrons' energy is used to drive a series of redox rxns that push H+ into inner membrane space

This is why NADH has higher ATP conversion vs FADH2 - NADH pushes more H+

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ubzw64PQPqM)
cards.front: How do NADH and FADH2 interact with the enzymes in the ETC to generate a proton gradient?

cards.back:
The redox rxn series have increasingly higher reduction potentials until Oxygen (final step with highest reduction potential)

*Higher reduction potential = stronger pull for electrons.*
**Electrons flow toward oxygen,** the final acceptor with the **highest reduction potential**.

Recall - **reduction potential is like how bad rxn wants to GAIN electrons**
So increasing reduction potentials spontaneously pull electrons through the chain

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1729.gif)
cards.front: How do electrons know to go down the Electron transport chain and not up it?

cards.back:
1. Complex **1** (NADH-CoQ oxioreductase)

2. Complex **2** (Succinate-CoQ Oxioreductase)

3. Complex **3** (CoQH2 -cytochrome c Oxioreductase)

4. Complex **4** (Cytochrome c Oxidase)

5. **ATP Synthase** (technically its own thing, but extremely closely linked to the ETC and often referred to as the 5th complex.)
![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2156.svg)

[YouTube Link](https://youtu.be/C8VHyezOJD4)
cards.front: What are the main components of the ETC?

cards.back:
Uses an **Iron-Sulfur cluster to transfer e-** from NADH to FMN and then CoenzymeQ

Results in pumping 4 protons and conversion of CoQ to CoQH2

**This is where NADH's start their journey through the ETC.**
![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2143.jpg)

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1868.png)

[YouTube Link](https://youtu.be/C8VHyezOJD4)
cards.front: Describe Complex I of the ETC

cards.back:
Uses an **Iron-Sulfer cluster to transfer e- **from succinate (in Kreb's cycle) to FAD to form FADH2

FADH2 then transfers electrons to CoQ forming CoQH2

FAD is not as high E as NADH so ***no protons are pumped into inner membrane space***

NOTE: Complex II is physically connected w/ Krebs cycle via succinate dehydrogenase

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1612.jpg)

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1870.gif) ![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1868.png)

[YouTube Link](https://youtu.be/C8VHyezOJD4)
cards.front: Describe Complex II of the ETC.

cards.back:
Just the chemical name for CoQH2

Because of the extra bonds to Hydrogen - this is a reduced molecule

-one = ketone = oxidized

-ol = Alcohol = reduced

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m596.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/test-prep/mcat/chemical-processes/alcohols-and-phenols/v/biologic-redox-reactions-of-alcohols-and-phenols)
cards.front: What is ubiquinol?

cards.back:
Chemical name for CoQ.

Because of the **extra bonds to oxygen**, this is an oxidized molecule.

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m596.jpg)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/test-prep/mcat/chemical-processes/alcohols-and-phenols/v/biologic-redox-reactions-of-alcohols-and-phenols)
cards.front: What is Ubiquinone?

cards.back:
2 step transfer of electrons from CoQH2 to a CoQ molecule within the ETC

This **then reduces cytochrome C in the inner membrane space**

Reason it happens is b/c CoQH2 has 2e- but can only transfer 1 at a time
Important thing to note is that e- provided by complex I and II are going to end up reducing cytochrom C
cards.front: What is the Q Cycle?

cards.back:
Uses an **iron sulfur cluster to transfer** electrons from CoQH2's to heme, **reducing cytochrome c** through the **Q cycle**.

Four protons are pumped into the inner membrane space at this point. ![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1200.png) ![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1868.png)

[YouTube Link](https://youtu.be/C8VHyezOJD4)
cards.front: Describe Complex III of the ETC.

cards.back:
Uses Cu2+ to transfer electrons from reduced cytochrome C to oxygen **via hydride bonds**
This forms water + finishes journey of electrons through ETC

Pumps 2 H+ into inner membrane space

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1117.png)

[YouTube Link](https://youtu.be/C8VHyezOJD4)
cards.front: Describe Complex IV of the ETC.

cards.back:
Glycolysis generates NADH in cytoplasm but it needs to get into matrix to interact w/ ETC

This is accomplished through two NADH shuttles:

1. Glycerol 3-phosphate shuttle

2. Malate-Aspartate Shuttle
cards.front: Describe the issue with the NADHs generated by glycolysis as they relate to the ETC.

cards.back:
In cytosol, version of glycerol-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (G3PD) oxidizes GHAP to glycerol-3-phosphate using cytosolic NADH

The glycerol-3-phosphate can then interact w/ special version G3PD that exists in inner membrane of mitochondria
This version uses an FAD as an electron acceptor

Causes glycerol-3 phosphate to be converted back to DHAP in cytosol, but this time electrons end up in inner membrane as FADH2 which can enter ETC at complex II

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2147.jpg)
cards.front: Describe the Glycerol 3 - Phosphate Shuttle

cards.back:
Cytosolic Oxaloacetate is converted to **Malate**, which* uses up a cytosolic NADH.*

Malate crosses into mitochondria, converted **back to oxaloacetate in matrix** --> ***produces an NADH***

Oxaloacetate then converted into aspartate which **exits** **mitochondria**

Allows for shuttling NADHs into and out of mitochondria as needed

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1851.jpg)

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ubzw64PQPqM)
cards.front: Describe the Malate-Aspartate Shuttle

cards.back: ![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1291.jpg)
cards.front: Describe the total ATP production of Aerobic Respiration

cards.back:
ATP synthase generates ATP from ADP using proton gradient - has two main portions:

**F0 portion**: Ion channel that allows H+ to flow down gradient from intermembrane space to the matrix

**F1 portion:** Uses energy released by gradient to phosphorylate ADP into ATP

cards.front: How are long-chain fatty acids absorbed?

HSL is an enzyme that breaks down TAGs **into fatty acids and glycerol for use as energy. **

HSL responds to low insulin levels, high epinephrine levels, and high cortisol, which all serve the common purpose of ***increasing blood sugar.

cards.front: What is Hormone Sensitive Lipase?

cards.back:
Triacylglycerol can only really be used to generate energy in the liver, but we store them all over our body.

Mobilization refers to the way we** transfer triacylglycerol break down products to the liver** so they can be Beta Oxidized.

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1029.jpg)
cards.front: What is meant by mobilization of triacylglycerols?

cards.back:
Lipoprotein lipase is necessary for the metabolism of **VLDL's and chylomicrons.**

It's function is to release free fatty acids from triacylglycerols in these lipoproteins.

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m15.png)

Albumin, the archetypal carrier protein, carries fatty acids.

cards.front: How are free fatty acids transported through the blood?

cards.back:
1. Very Low Density Lipoproteins (VLDL)

2. Intermediate Density Lipoproteins (IDL)

3. Low Density Lipoproteins (LDL)

4. High Density Lipoproteins (HDL)

cards.front: What are the different types of Lipoproteins?

cards.back:
Triacylglycerols and cholesterols are transported through protein/lipid complexes called lipoproteins of varying density.
![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m341.jpg)

cards.front: How are triacylglycerol and cholesterols transported through the blood?

cards.back:
A chylomicron is a highly soluble transporter of dietary lipids to other tissues.

**Assembly** of chylomicrons **occurs in the intestinal lining.**

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1972.gif)

[Khan Academy Link](https://www.khanacademy.org/test-prep/mcat/biomolecules/fat-and-protein-metabolism/v/digestion-mobilization-and-transport-of-fats-part-i)
cards.front: What is a chylomicron?

cards.back:
A VLDL is a similar structure to a chylomicron; however, these are **assembled and produced in liver cells. **

The main function of VLDL's is to transport triacylglycerols to other tissues.

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2768.jpg)

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PkKH8lTxvzA)
cards.front: What is a VLDL?

cards.back:
An IDL is a VLDL after it has been emptied of its triacylglycerols.

IDLs are **either reabsobred by the liver** to make more VLDL's or **further processed downstream to become even higher density Lipoproteins

** ![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2768.jpg)

cards.front: Chylomicrons and VLDL are primarily {{c1::triacylglycerol::triacylglycerol or cholesterol}} carriers?

LDLs are lipoproteins that specialize in carrying cholesterol through the body

cards.front: What is a LDL?

cards.back:
HDL's are synthesized in the liver and intestines and released as dense,** protein rich** particles into the blood.

HDL** contains apolipoproteins **that help it clean the blood vessels of extra cholesterol.

For this reason, HDL is considered "good" cholesterol.

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2768.jpg)

cards.back:
Also referred to as apoproteins, they form the protein component of lipoproteins and play important roles in determining and regulating their function.

cards.front: What is an apolipoprotein?

cards.back: Cholesterol can be obtained through dietary sources or **synthesized** **in the liver.**
cards.front: What are the main ways we obtain cholesterol?

cards.back:
Fatty acids are written like so *
*
*carbons:double bonds omega#*
*
*
Carbons refer to the number of carbons in the fatty acid.

Double bonds refers to the number of double bonds in the fatty acid.

***Omega# ***is a number that designates how close to the 1 carbon the closest double bond is.

For example, a 20 carbon fatty acid with 5 double bonds, the closest of which is at carbon 3, would be called C20:5 omega3.

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1095.jpg)
cards.front: How are fatty acids named?

cards.back:
Excess acetyl-CoA (after a large meal perhaps) must be transferred to the cytoplasm from the matrix using a series of enzymes.

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m791.jpg)
cards.front: What must happen to acetyl-CoA before it can be used in fatty acid synthesis?

cards.back:
Acetyl-CoA Carboxylase uses biotin, ATP, and CO2 to form malonyl-CoA

This is one of the first steps of fatty acid synthesis.

This **enzyme is activated by insulin and citrate.**

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m690.jpg)

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z5SMNesTN90)
cards.front: Describe Acetyl-CoA Carboxylase

cards.back:
Fatty Acid Synthase (AKA Palmitate Synthase) is a large multienzmye complex that uses NADPH to add 2 carbon fragments to malonyl-CoA.

This **happens over and over until the fatty acid is 16 carbons long (Palmitate).**

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m114.jpg)
cards.front: Describe Fatty Acid Synthase

cards.back:
Understand that they are basically just the exact opposite of one another.

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1747.png)

cards.front: How can one easily understand Beta Oxidation and Fatty Acid synthesis?

cards.back: Three fatty acids are attached to glycerol in the **liver** and **adipose** **tissue**.
cards.front: How are triacylglycerols synthesized from fatty acids?

cards.back:
Beta oxidation is the process of breaking down Fatty Acids into **acetyl CoA** for *use in the citric acid cycle. *

Just like Fatty Acid Synthesis, it is a cycle of reactions that produces NADH and **liberates 2 carbon fragments of the fatty acid at a time.**

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1940.jpg)

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=__jS-pjzb5k)
cards.front: What is beta oxidation?

cards.back:
No!

They both require special enzymes --> **Isomerases** and **reductases**

Purpose is to unsaturate/unbranch the FAs so they can be β oxidized normally
cards.front: Can branched or unsaturated fatty acids be oxidized normally?

cards.back: [YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=__jS-pjzb5k)

cards.front: Fatty acid synthesis occurs in the {{c1::cytoplasm::mitochondria or cytoplasm?}}

cards.back:
1. Activation

2. Fatty Acid Entry into Mitochondria

3. Beta Oxidation
cards.front: What are three main steps of fatty acid catabolism?

cards.back:
Fatty acid **must first be activated by** fatty-acyl-CoA Synthetase

This enzyme **attaches a CoA to the fatty acid.**

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m743.jpg)
cards.front: What does it mean to say a fatty acid is activated?

cards.back:
Short-chain and medium chain (2 to 12 carbons) **diffuse freely into the mitochondria.**
Long chain (14-20 carbons) fatty acids require transport via a **carnitine shuttle.**

This *transferring step is slow, and actually serves as the rate limiting step of β oxidation.*

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m517.jpg)

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=__jS-pjzb5k)
cards.front: How do activated fatty acids enter the mitochondria?

cards.back:
It is actually the same up until the final cycle. For even numbered fatty acids, the **final cleavage of the 4 carbon molecule will result in two acetyl-CoAs. **
However,*** for odd numbered fatty acids***, the final cleavage of the 5 carbon molecule will result in an **acetyl-CoA** and a **propionyl-CoA.**

This Propionyl-CoA Undergoes a series of reactions to **form succinyl-CoA**, which can then enter the citric acid cycle.

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m265.jpg)

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=__jS-pjzb5k)
cards.front: How is the beta oxidation of odd numbered fatty acids different?

cards.back:
Ketone bodies are essentially transportable forms of acetyl-CoA that the **liver produces to feed other tissues ***during prolonged periods of starvation
*
[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dbno1Aa-E_4)
cards.front: What are ketone bodies?

cards.back:
1. Acetoacetate

2. 3-hydroxybutyrate

3. Acetone (**doesn't really get metabolized**, *more of a byproduct*)

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1466.jpg)

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dbno1Aa-E_4)
cards.front: What are the three main ketone bodies?

cards.back:
Ketogenesis is the process of creating ketone bodies from excess acetyl-CoA in the liver.

HMG-CoA ***Synthetase*** converts **Acetyl-CoA** to HMG-CoA

Then HMG-CoA ***lyase*** converts **HMG-CoA** into acetoacetate (a ketone body)

Acetoacetate then sent to tissues in need or reduced to 3-hydroxybutyrate (another ketone body)

**Acetone is byproduct of this rxn** --> *not metabolically active*

![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1928.jpg)

[YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dbno1Aa-E_4)
cards.front: What is Ketogenesis?

cards.back: [YouTube Link](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dbno1Aa-E_4)
cards.front: Ketogenesis occurs in the {{c1::mitochondria::mitochondria or cytoplasm}} of liver cells.

cards.back:
Breakdown of ketone bodies for energy

3-hydroxybutyrate → oxidized to acetoacetate, **releasing NADH** (this occurs in *mitochondria of needy tissue*)

Acetoacetate gets activated by **thiophorase** to make acetoacetyl-CoA **which is cleaved** **into** 2 acetyl-CoA.

*Liver lacks thiophorase so it can't burn ketone bodies it makes* --> helps liver serve as energy supplier for rest of body

Mechanisms:

→ overall → mobilizes energy stores & maintains high blood sugar during prolonged stress

cards.front: What effect do the glucocorticoids have on metabolism?

cards.back:
Purpose → prepare body for “fight-or-flight” by ↑ blood glucose levels

Mechanisms:

→ stimulate glycogenolysis in liver & muscle → release glucose for energy

→ stimulate lipolysis in adipose tissue → release fatty acids for fuel

→ inhibit insulin & stimulate glucagon → reduce glucose uptake, maintain high blood sugar

→ act on heart & other target organs → ↑ heart rate, contractility, and basal metabolic rate

All effects → mobilize stored energy & ensure rapid fuel availability for stress response

Triiodothyronine (T3) produces a rapid increase in metabolic rate that is short lived.

cards.front: {{c1::Defense mechanisms}} are {{c2::a way to protect ourselves from unconscious wants, feelings, desires, and impulses}}
The four types of defense mechanisms are {{c1::pathological}}, {{c1::immature}}, {{c1::mature}}, and {{c1::neurotic}}
**Pathological defense mechanisms** are defense mechanisms that {{c1::distort reality}}
The **pathological defense mechanisms** are {{c1::denial}}

cards.back:
*
**Ex; if someone has breast cancer, they just deny the fact that they do*
cards.front: {{c2::Denial}} is {{c1::a pathological defense mechanism where a person pretends something hasn't happened}}.

cards.back: *mnemonic: it is immature to say pp*
cards.front: The **immature defense mechanisms** include {{c2::projection}} and {{c2::passive aggression}}

cards.back:
*
**ex: if you just failed a test and are feeling particularly stupid you go and call your dog “stupid” and “dumb”*
cards.front: {{c1::Projection}} is {{c2::an immature defense mechanism where an individual attributes unwanted thoughts and feelings onto another person. }}

cards.back:
*
**ex: You feel stupid so you call someone else stupid and then they begin to feel stupid overtime*
cards.front: {{c1::Projective identification}} is when {{c2::a person targeted with projection can start believing and having thoughts of the attributes projected on to them}}.

cards.back:
*
**example: Your roommate leaves a bunch of dishes and then asks you to go to the bar. You say ''well I would but I actually have a TON of dishes to do today for some reason! crazy how they just pile up!''*
*
*
cards.front: {{c1::Passive aggression}} is {{c2::an immature defense mechanism where you passively express anger towards someone}}

cards.back: mnemonic: 4R ID
cards.front: The **neurotic defense mechanisms** include {{c1::intellectualization}},{{c1::rationalization}}, {{c1::regression}}, {{c1::repression}}, {{c1::displacement}}, and {{c1::reaction formation}}

cards.back:
*
*
**can involve false logic and false reasoning*

**example: I had to cheat on the test because the professor made it impossible*
cards.front: {{c1::Rationalization}} is {{c2::a neurotic defense mechanism that involves making yourself believe you were not at fault}}

cards.back:
*
*
**not necessarily a BABY per se but an earlier stage of development*

cards.back:

cards.back:

cards.back:
*

cards.front: {{c1::Reaction formation}} is {{c2::a neurotic defense mechanism where someone goes beyond denial and begins behaving in the opposite way to which they think or feel}}

cards.back: ![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1227.gif)
cards.front: {{c1::Norms}} are {{c2::standards for what behaviors are acceptable/unacceptable and are typically set by groups of individuals}}

cards.back:
*
**ex: You yell loud at baseball games when something good happens but you probably wouldnt do that in your office*
*
*
*ex: People in USA greet with handshakes but in Europe a kiss on the cheek is more common*
cards.front: **Norms **vary depending on {{c1::context}}, {{c1::location}}, and {{c1::culture}}
**Norms **are reinforced by {{c1::sanctions}}
{{c1::Sanctions}} are {{c2::rewards/punishments for behaviors in accord with or against norms}}
Positive sanction = {{c1::a reward for conforming to norms}}
Negative sanction = {{c1::a punishment for violating norms}}

cards.back:
*
**ex: going to jail for breaking the law*
cards.front: Formal sanction = {{c1::officially recognized and enforced sanction}}

cards.back:
*
**ex: compliments from peers, frowns, insults, parents yelling at you*
cards.front: Informal sanction = {{c1::unofficially recognized sanction that does not result in specific punishment}}
**Formal norms **are {{c1::established written rules}} and are {{c1::typically strictly enforced}}

cards.back:
*
**these dictate appropriate behavior w/o the need for written rules*
*
*
*deviating from these norms won't get you thrown in jail, but may lead to a bad reputation*
cards.front: **Informal norms** are {{c1::understood norms that are less precise w/o specific punishments}}

cards.back:
*
**example: common courtesy to tell ur friend their zipper is down*
*
*
*not engaging in these norms does not result in sever consequences, no actual punishment*
cards.front: **Folkways **are {{c1::the mildest type of norm}} and are {{c1::the rules/manners we are supposed to follow}}

cards.back:
*
*
*Ex: friends takes of shirt who has painted baseball team’s logo on chest. You feel strongly about modesty so you think its wrong that your friend took of shirt and is exposing skin. No serious consequences of your friend’s behavior other than your disapproval*
cards.front: **Mores **are {{c1::norms based on moral value/belief that usually elicit a strong reaction when violated but still no serious consequences}}

cards.back:
*
**ex: Streaking on the field at a highschool football game will get you arrested. However, there may not be severe outrage from this. Some people will feel grossed out but there will be some people who laugh and cheer*
cards.front: **Laws **are {{c1::norms based on right/wrong with formal consequences for deviation that may/may not cause outrage}}

cards.back: example: incest and cannibalism
cards.front: **Taboos **are {{c1::behaviors completely forbidden/wrong to where deviation typically results in severe disgust and possible legal action}}
{{c2::Deviance}} is when {{c1::a norm is violated}}

cards.back:
*
**as long as you are behaving differently from the societal norms, you are deviant*
*
*
*ex: vegans*
*most americans eat meat, but vegans aren't bad or anything, just deviant from the norm*
cards.front: **Deviance **does not have to be {{c1::negative}}

{{c1::Symbolic interactionism}} states that {{c2::society is a byproduct of everyday interactions of individuals}} and that {{c2::looking at everyday behaviors}} helps us better understand and define deviance

cards.back:
*
**Ex: elite athlete who grows up believing that cheating is wrong and to be a successful athlete one must train hard, avoid drugs and alcohol, and be respectful to opponents. Elite athlete now switches teams and now new team member believe that using steroids, partying, and heckling is the best way to be successful at a sport. Perhaps even show athlete how to be deviant by demonstrating how to take a particular drug, introducing athlete to steroid, etc. Overtime the athlete will learn from the new team members that these behaviors (partying, heckling, and drug use) are acceptable even though they were not before. Accepts these new deviant behaviors overtime*
cards.front: {{c1::The Theory of Differential Association::Theory}} states that {{c2::deviance is a learned behavior that results from continuous exposure to others whom violate norms/laws}}.

cards.back:
*
**Deviance depends entirely on what's acceptable in society*
*
*

*
**example, a pigeon that has been reinforced to peck an electronic button. During its training history, every time the pigeon pecked the button, it will have received a small amount of bird seed as a reinforcer. So, whenever the bird is hungry, it will peck the button to receive food. However, if the button were to be turned off, the hungry pigeon will first try pecking the button just as it has in the past. When no food is forthcoming, the bird will likely try again ... and again, and again. After a period of frantic activity, in which their pecking behavior yields no result, the pigeon's pecking will decrease in frequency.*

*

*example 2: a baby cries to get moms attention, when it doesn't get it immediately, it cries even more and louder as a last ditch effort (extinction burst). When this fails to get moms attention, it stops crying.*

cards.back:
1. **Pre-Conventional **(pre-adolescent)

- 1. ***Obedience vs. Punishment*** – reasoning is based on physical consequences of actions, so obeying the rules is a means to avoid punishment.

- 2. ***Individualism and Exchange*** – recognize not just one right view by authorities, different individuals have different viewpoints.
![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m1258.jpg)

2. **Conventional **

- 3. ***Good Boy and Good Girl*** - Authority is internalized, but not questioned, and reasoning is based on group person belongs. Individual is good in order to be seen as good by others, emphasis on conformity.

- 4. ***Law and Order*** – maintaining social order, child is aware of wider roles of society and obeying laws.
![](https://qyjmivntajbigjswhahb.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/starter-deck-media/captain-hook/m2029.jpg)

3. **Post-Conventional **(moral)
- 5. ***Social Contract*** – Individual becomes aware that even though rules and laws exist for greater good, there are times this law works against interest of particular people.
· Ex. for Heinz, is protection of life more important than breaking/stealing? People at this stage said yes.
- 6. ***Universal Ethical Principle*** – people develop own set of moral guidelines, which may or may not fit the law, and principles apply to everyone. People who uphold and believe in these have to be prepared to act towards these even if they have to obey consequences. Very few people who reach this stage, ex. Ghandi.
